chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter opens with the queen's locker puzzle and lets the answer, the square numbers, lead into everything else. Each idea starts with a prediction (will this locker stay open, can a square end in 7, how many cubes make this block), then a picture or a pattern explains why. Squares come first, as areas, digits and sums of odd numbers; then square roots by three methods and by estimation; then the same journey for cubes.

points.title: Predict, then check
points.text: Every concept opens with a question the student answers before the video reveals it, such as which lockers stay open or whether 2032 can be a square.

points.title: Pictures that prove
points.text: Squares are drawn as tiles and cubes as stacks of unit cubes, and the odd number pattern is shown with inverted L shapes, so each rule is seen before it is used.

points.title: One tool, one idea
points.text: Ten tools, each used once, appear only where handling the objects is the idea itself: lockers and squares, building squares and cubes, odd-number corners, the gap between squares, finding a side from an area, pairing and tripling prime factors, trapping a root between two whole numbers, and a ladder of differences.

points.title: Several roads to a root
points.text: Square roots are found by listing squares, by subtracting odd numbers, by pairing prime factors and by estimating with nearby squares, and the student learns when each road is quickest.

concepts.concept_name: A hundred lockers and a hidden treasure

content.text:
Queen Ratnamanjuri of Khoisnam left a will. Her treasure was kept in one of the 100 lockers in her palace, all closed and locked.
100 people were called one after another. The first person opened every locker. The second person closed every second locker: locker 2, 4, 6, and so on. The third person toggled every third locker: if it was open it was closed, and if it was closed it was opened. The fourth person toggled every fourth locker, and so on, until the hundredth person toggled locker 100.
After all 100 people had done this, which lockers remain open?
Hint: Find the number of times each locker is toggled.

content.text:
1. Predict first: after all 100 people have passed, do you think most lockers end open, most end closed, or only a few end open?
2. Try a small case by hand: 10 lockers and 10 people. Keep a record of which lockers each person touches.
3. A locker that is touched an odd number of times ends open; an even number of times, closed.
4. So the real question is: how many times is each locker touched? Keep that question open for the next topic.

concepts.concept_name: Each toggle is a factor

content.text:
Locker 6 is toggled by person 1, person 2, person 3 and person 6. These are exactly the factors of 6.
Each factor of 6 has a partner factor: 1 × 6 and 2 × 3.
Does every number have an even number of factors?
Write the factors of 1, 4 and 9 in the boxes.

content.text:
1. Predict first: who toggles locker 12? Write the list before you check.
2. Person k toggles locker 12 exactly when k divides 12, so the toggles are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12: the factors.
3. Factors come in partner pairs: 1 × 12, 2 × 6, 3 × 4. Six factors, six toggles: closed.
4. Now look at 1, 4 and 9. Does every factor still have a different partner?

content.text:
Worked example: How many times is locker 12 toggled, and does it end open or closed?
1. Locker 12 is toggled by every person whose number divides 12.
2. The factors of 12 pair up: 12 = 1 × 12 = 2 × 6 = 3 × 4.
3. That is 6 factors, so locker 12 is toggled 6 times.
4. An even number of toggles brings it back to closed.
Answer: 6 times, so locker 12 ends closed

concepts.concept_name: Squares have an odd number of factors

content.text:
Can you use this insight to find more numbers with an odd number of factors?
For 36: 1 × 36, 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9 and 6 × 6. The factor 6 is paired with itself.
Numbers like 1 × 1, 2 × 2, 3 × 3, 4 × 4 are called square numbers.
Square numbers have an odd number of factors.

content.text:
1. Predict first: does 36 have an odd or an even number of factors?
2. List the pairs: 1 × 36, 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9, 6 × 6. The last pair uses 6 twice.
3. So 36 has 9 factors, an odd number. This happens only when a number is some number times itself.
4. Such numbers, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and so on, are square numbers.

Worked example: Count the factors of 36 and say why the count is odd.
1. Write the factor pairs: 36 = 1 × 36 = 2 × 18 = 3 × 12 = 4 × 9 = 6 × 6.
2. The factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18 and 36.
3. That is 9 factors, because 6 pairs with itself and is counted once.
Answer: 36 has 9 factors; the odd count comes from 6 × 6

concepts.concept_name: Practice: solve the locker puzzle

content.text:
The queen's will also had a clue: the first five lockers that were touched exactly twice hold the code. Which are these five lockers?
A locker touched exactly twice has exactly two factors, 1 and itself. So these are the prime numbers 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11.

content.text:
The locker puzzle (the secret code): The first five lockers that were touched exactly twice hold the code to the treasure. Which are these five lockers?
1. Each person who touches a locker is a factor of its number.
2. Touched exactly twice means exactly two factors: 1 and the number itself.
3. A number with exactly two factors is a prime number. 1 has one factor and 4 has three.
4. The first five primes are 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11.
Answer: Lockers 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students list the people who toggle a given locker, recognise them as the factors of the locker number, and pair each factor with its partner factor.
Students find the numbers whose factors do not all pair with a different partner, explain that a factor multiplied by itself has no separate partner, and name such numbers square numbers.
Students list the lockers that stay open after all 100 people pass as the square numbers up to 100.
Students decide for any locker number how many times it is toggled by counting its factors, and find the lockers touched exactly twice as the prime numbers.

concepts.concept_name: A square number is an area

content.text:
1.1 Square Numbers
The area of a square of side 1 unit is 1 sq unit, of side 2 units is 4 sq units, of side 3 units is 9 sq units. For sides 4, 5 and 10 the areas are 16, 25 and 100 sq units.
A square of side n units has area n × n = n² sq units, read as n squared.
We can square fractions and decimals too: (3/5)² = 9/25 and 2.5² = 6.25.
Numbers like 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 which are squares of natural numbers are called perfect squares.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a square has side 6 units. Is its area 12 square units or 36 square units?
2. Area is side times side: 6 × 6 = 36, written 6², read 6 squared. Squaring is not doubling.
3. Fractions and decimals square the same way: (3/5)² = 9/25 and 2.5² = 6.25.
4. Squares of natural numbers, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, are called perfect squares.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the areas of squares with sides 6 units, 3/5 unit and 2.5 units.
1. Side 6: 6² = 6 × 6 = 36 square units.
2. Side 3/5: (3/5)² = 9/25 square unit.
3. Side 2.5: 2.5² = 2.5 × 2.5 = 6.25 square units.
4. Only 36 is a perfect square, because only 6 is a natural number.
Answer: 36, 9/25 and 6.25 square units

concepts.concept_name: The last digit of a square

content.text:
Fill in the table of squares from 1 to 30.
What patterns do you notice? The squares end only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9.
If a number ends in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9, is it always a square? No: 26 ends in 6 but is not a square.
Write 5 numbers such that by looking at their units digit it can be said that they are not squares.
1², 9², 11², 19², 21², 29² all end in 1. Write the next two squares ending in 1.
If a number has 1 or 9 in the units place, its square ends in 1.
The squares 16, 36, 196, 256, 576 and 676 end in 6. Which of 38², 34², 46², 56², 74², 82² have 6 in the units place?
Find more such patterns by observing the numbers and their squares in the table.

content.text:
1. Predict first: can a perfect square end in 7?
2. Only the last digit of a number decides the last digit of its square. Squaring 0 to 9 gives last digits 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4, 1.
3. So squares end only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. A number ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 is never a square.
4. The converse fails: 26 ends in 6 but is not a square. A last digit can rule a square out, never in.
5. A number ending in 4 or 6 has a square ending in 6; ending in 1 or 9, a square ending in 1.

content.text:
Worked example: Which of 38², 34², 46², 56², 74² and 82² end in 6?
1. Only the last digit matters: 38 and 82 end in 8 or 2, and 8² = 64 and 2² = 4 end in 4.
2. 34 and 74 end in 4, and 4² = 16 ends in 6.
3. 46 and 56 end in 6, and 6² = 36 ends in 6.
4. Check one: 34² = 1156, which ends in 6.
Answer: 34², 46², 56² and 74² end in 6; 38² and 82² end in 4

concepts.concept_name: Squares that end in 1, and numbers that cannot be squares

content.text:
1. Predict first: what are the next two squares ending in 1 after 29²?
2. Numbers ending in 1 or 9 have squares ending in 1, so the next are 31² and 39².
3. Numbers ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 can never be squares.

Worked example: Write the next two squares ending in 1 after 29², and five numbers that cannot be squares.

concepts.concept_name: Zeros at the end and odd or even

content.text:
10² = 100, 20² = 400, 100² = 10000.
If a number ends in 3 zeros, how many zeros will its square have at the end?
Notice the number of zeros at the end of a number and its square. Is this pattern always true? Can we say that squares can only have an even number of zeros at the end?
What can we say about the parity of a number and its square?

lines: If a number ends in 3 zeros, how many zeros will its square have at the end?
Notice the number of zeros at the end of a number and its square. Is this pattern always true? Can we say that squares can only have an even number of zeros at the end?
What can we say about the parity of a number and its square?

content.text:
1. Predict first: 3000 ends in 3 zeros. How many zeros end 3000²?
2. 3000² = 3000 × 3000. Each factor brings 3 zeros, so the square ends in 6 zeros: 9000000.
3. The zeros double, so a perfect square always ends in an even number of zeros.
4. Odd times odd is odd and even times even is even, so a number and its square have the same parity.

1. 3000² = 3000 × 3000 = 9000000.
2. 3 zeros from each factor give 3 + 3 = 6 zeros at the end.
3. 3000 is even, and even × even is even, so 3000² is even.
Answer: 6 zeros, and 3000² is even

content.text:
Figure it Out (square numbers, question 2): Which of the following numbers have the digit 4 in the units place? (i) 64² (ii) 108² (iii) 292² (iv) 36²
1. Only the last digit of each number matters.
2. 64 and 36 end in 4 and 6, and 4² = 16 and 6² = 36 both end in 6.
3. 108 and 292 end in 8 and 2, and 8² = 64 and 2² = 4 both end in 4.
4. So 108² and 292² end in 4.
Answer: (ii) 108² and (iii) 292²

media.title: Square Builder
media.context: CBSE Class 8, A Square and A Cube, the opening of the square. NCERT Ganita Prakash builds squares on a DOT GRID and the older NCERT builds them as unit-square AREA; this tool reads the grid as unit tiles, which is legible in both. It sits BEFORE the square root is introduced in this same chapter, so the radical sign never appears and the reverse direction is asked as 'what is its side?', never as 'find the root'. Products are written with U+00D7. The chapter's own odd-number-sum pattern (1, 1+3, 1+3+5) IS the L-shaped border arithmetically, and the tool names them as the same fact.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the filled square or the rule test table that explains it.
whatYouLearned: A square of side n holds n times n tiles, written n squared
Squaring is not doubling; the two agree only at side 2
Stepping the side up by one adds 2n plus 1 tiles, so the growth is never fixed

overview.goal: The student predicts and then verifies the tile count of an n by n square, and writes n squared as a rule that survives testing at n equal to 5, 9 and 25.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground, the way squared paper sits on a desk, with the tile array as the only object on it. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class argues that seven squared is fourteen, and the square itself is asked to settle it.
overview.concept: A square of side n is an n by n array of unit tiles, so it holds n times n tiles. That count is written n squared. Because the figure is a square, width always equals height, so one number n fixes the whole picture and the tile count follows from it.
overview.purpose: The student predicts and then verifies the tile count of an n by n square, and writes n squared as a rule that survives testing at n equal to 5, 9 and 25.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Square fills the main panel with the side readout above it and the tile count directly beneath. The n and n squared table sits to the right on a wide frame and collapses to a single scrolling strip under the square on a 390 px frame. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the tile count, the table or the rule while a prediction is still open. The count IS the answer.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Filling the square row by row gives n rows of n tiles, which is n added to itself n times, that is n times n. Stepping the side from n to n plus 1 adds an L shaped border of two arms of n and one corner tile, so the count grows by 2n plus 1 and never by a fixed amount, which is exactly why doubling cannot be the rule. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A single tile is a legal square, and 1 is the one side whose count does not grow. conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the square at side 7 drawn as an empty outline with the count hidden, and ask the class to predict the tile count out loud. Commit the class number on the prediction pad. Target side 7. Never fill before the prediction is committed, and never say 49 at this call. Call 2. Fill the square row by row and let the true count land beside the committed guess. Point at the count readout. Target side 7, seven rows. Say what the gap between guess and count is, never whether the class was right or wrong. Call 3. Step the side from 7 to 8 and light the added L shaped border. Point at the two arms and then at the single corner tile. Targets side 8, and the border of 15. Read the added count from the tool's own readout, never from memory.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Each row holds n tiles because the figure is square, so width equals height
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The count climbs by a whole row each time a row lands, not by one tile
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: n squared is n groups of n, which is why it is a multiplication and not an addition

observationsAndConclusions.why: n times n equals 2 times n only when n is 2, so the two rules cross at exactly one point
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Side 2 is the one side where doubling gives the right answer
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A rule that is right once is not right; agreement at one value proves nothing

observationsAndConclusions.why: The outer square minus the inner square is 2n plus 1 tiles
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Stepping the side up adds an L of two arms and one corner
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The step grows with n, so the count cannot be produced by doubling anything

media.description: A square of unit tiles stands on a plain working ground with one drag handle that moves its width and its height together, so a single number n fixes the whole picture. The array fills one row at a time from the bottom, the count climbing by a whole row rather than by a tile, and a running table of n against n squared builds beside it on a wide pane. Stepping the side up by one lights the added L shaped border in a second colour, drawn as three separately counted pieces - an arm of n, a second arm of n, and one corner tile that lands last - so 2n + 1 is watched rather than asserted, and the same number is named as the next odd number, which is the textbook's own explanation of the growth. A claimed count that cannot be a square is drawn as tiles that RUN OUT inside the ruled grid, with a bracket strip placing it between the two whole sides that bracket it, so the doubling error is refuted by a picture of an unfinishable square rather than by a red cross. Above side 12 the tiles stop being drawn and the square becomes a labelled outline carrying its count, which is where the rule has to take over from counting. A typed rule is parsed to a small expression tree - never eval - and run against the tool's own ground truth at n equal to 5, 9 and 25, with every disagreeing row washed in the second colour, because agreement at a single value is not a rule.

source_tool.name: Square Builder
source_tool.blurb: a grid grows from 1 by 1 to 12 by 12 as the student drags a side handle, and the newly added L shaped border shows what each step adds
source_tool.description: The student predicts and then verifies the tile count of an n by n square, and writes n squared as a rule that survives testing at n equal to 5, 9 and 25.

modes.ai: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens on a 4 by 4 grid with the tile count HIDDEN and asks the class to predict how many small tiles a side of 7 will hold. Beat 2 fills the square one row at a time and the count lands beside the guess. Beat 3 steps the side up once and lights the added L shaped border in the second colour, so what each step adds is watchable before anyone writes a rule. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setSide, fillRows, highlightLShape and say. No drag: the agent cannot sweep a continuous control with finite calls.
modes.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the side from its own numbers, shows the question, then reveals the filled square, the running n and n squared table and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.

whatYouLearned: A square of side n holds n times n tiles, written n squared
Squaring is not doubling; the two agree only at side 2
Stepping the side up by one adds 2n plus 1 tiles, so the growth is never fixed

concept.notation: Write n squared, read as 'n squared' or 'n to the power 2'. The raised 2 counts how many factors of n are multiplied, it is not a multiplier.
concept.statement: A square of side n is an n by n array of unit tiles, so it holds n times n tiles. That count is written n squared. Because the figure is a square, width always equals height, so one number n fixes the whole picture and the tile count follows from it.
prerequisites: area of a rectangle as length times breadth from Class 7
misconceptions: Squaring read as doubling, so 7 squared is taken as 14. The array makes 14 impossible to draw as a square.
Reading the raised 2 as 'times 2' rather than as a count of equal factors.
concept.why_it_is_true: Filling the square row by row gives n rows of n tiles, which is n added to itself n times, that is n times n. Stepping the side from n to n plus 1 adds an L shaped border of two arms of n and one corner tile, so the count grows by 2n plus 1 and never by a fixed amount, which is exactly why doubling cannot be the rule.
worked_numbers: side 4 gives 4 rows of 4, so 16 tiles; doubling would have said 8.
side 7 gives 49 tiles; the doubling answer 14 is smaller than one row of the square plus its neighbour.
side 12 gives 144 tiles, the largest square the grid draws before it switches to an outline.

answer_key.worked: A square of side n holds n times n tiles, written n squared. The count is the area of the square in unit tiles.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn square: the tile count for the stated side, the side for the stated count, or whether the typed rule agrees with n squared at every tested n.
answer_key.precision: Integer arithmetic only. No floating point value decides a tile count or a side, and no rule is graded by string comparison.
answer_key.ground_truth: tiles(n) = n * n, computed as an integer product. side(t) = the integer s with s*s === t, found by integer search, or null when no such s exists. ruleAgrees(text) = parse the typed rule to a small expression tree and evaluate it at n = 5, 9 and 25, comparing each value with n*n.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: A single tile. It is a legal square and the smallest one, and the table starts at 1 and 1 so the student sees that squaring leaves 1 unmoved. Never treat it as an empty scene.

edge_cases.case: A tile count that is not a perfect square
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The tool refuses to draw it as a square and says why, showing the two whole sides it falls between. It never rounds a side to make the picture work.
The grid is drawn as an outline with the side labelled and no individual tiles, so counting is impossible and the rule has to be used. The tool says on screen that the tiles are not drawn.

edge_cases.case: A rule that happens to agree at one n
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Agreement at a single value never closes the stage. The rule is run at n equal to 5, 9 and 25 and the first row that disagrees is named, because one case is not a proof.

edge_cases.case: A prediction typed before any side is chosen
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The prediction box stays locked until a side is set, so a guess is always a guess about a stated square rather than about nothing.

questions.description: Replaces the built in practice bank. Items are {kind:'count_tiles', n:number} | {kind:'find_side', tiles:number} | {kind:'state_rule', testAt:number[]} | {kind:'choice', prompt, options[], correct, explain}.

showTable.description: Show the running table of n against n squared beside the square. Hidden in Stage 3 so the rule has to be used rather than read off.

startingSide.description: The side the square opens on, clamped 1 to 12.

constraints: The figure stays a square at every moment: width always equals height, and a drag that would separate them is refused rather than corrected silently.
Tiles stay whole and non overlapping. No partial tile is ever drawn to make a count come out.
The tile count is computed as an integer product n * n, never accumulated by counting rendered rects, so a redraw cannot drift.
Render is capped at 144 tiles. Above a side of 12 the square switches to a labelled outline and the tool says the tiles are not drawn.
A typed rule is parsed to a small expression tree and evaluated numerically, never passed to eval, so 2n plus 1 style input is safe and n times n and n squared both pass.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: The square, the teacher caption, the prediction pad, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: the grid is drawn at side 7 as an empty outline with the count hidden. The class commits a tile count out loud and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.

Step: the side moves from 7 to 8 and the added L shaped border lights in the second colour, two arms of 7 and one corner, so the step of 15 is seen rather than stated.

play_modes: DOUBLING HUNT: find every side from 1 to 12 whose tile count is double the side, then say why the list cannot be longer.
L SHAPE HUNT: step the side up three times and name the size of each new border before it lights.
RULE BREAKER: find a rule that survives n equal to 5 and fails by n equal to 25.
BUILD YOUR OWN: set any side in range, predict the count, then let the tool check the prediction.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example setting the side a child names and filling it row by row to settle an argument.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

visual_behaviour.never: Do not show the tile count, the table or the rule while a prediction is still open. The count IS the answer.
visual_behaviour.scene: A square array of unit tiles on a plain ground, one drag handle on the right side and one on the bottom moving together. Filled tiles carry the primary accent; the L shaped border added by the last step carries the second accent; the outline stays a thin uniform stroke.
visual_behaviour.layout: Square fills the main panel with the side readout above it and the tile count directly beneath. The n and n squared table sits to the right on a wide frame and collapses to a single scrolling strip under the square on a 390 px frame.
readouts: Tile count, live once the prediction has been committed
Tiles added by the last step, whenever the side has just changed
animations: Row fill: each row of tiles fades in left to right over 180 ms, staggered 60 ms per row, so the count reads as n groups of n rather than as a block appearing.
L shaped border: on a step up the two arms sweep out from the corner and the single corner tile lands last with one pulse, which is the moment 2n plus 1 becomes visible.
Prediction compare: the committed guess slides in beside the true count and the difference between them is drawn as a short bar rather than announced as right or wrong.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: Tile size is derived from the panel width and n so every tile stays at least 12 px on a side; above a side of 12 the tiles are dropped entirely and the square is drawn as a labelled outline rather than shrunk further.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The array has to be seen filling before n squared is written down, or the rule arrives as a symbol to memorise rather than as a count the student has just made

tool_config.image_prompts_note: Empty by design. This mount is a mechanism, not a depiction, and the standard mandates hand-built inline SVG with no external asset dependency, so no depictive picture is declared.
mathematical_facts: A square of side n holds n times n tiles, written n squared
The raised 2 counts how many equal factors are multiplied; it is not a multiplier
Stepping the side from n to n plus 1 adds 2n plus 1 tiles, never a fixed amount

question_integration.test: Freeze any injected step and ask: could the teacher read every number in this question off THIS screen? If not, fix the scene, not the words.
question_integration.parse_rule: Read the side out of the question text (the first integer described as a side, an edge or a length) and set n to it. If the question states a tile count or an area instead, read that and set n to its integer square root, drawing the square only when the root is whole. The square drawn must contain every number the question mentions.
question_integration.compute_rule: Build the scene from the parsed numbers, then compute the answer with the tool's own ground truth function ON THE DRAWN SCENE. Never carry the bank's answer as truth while drawing a different scene. The two must agree by construction; if they disagree the scene is wrong, not the bank.
question_integration.learn_source: props.learnQuestions (delivery_mode = 'Learn'). Mandatory checkpoints (stickers.mandatory_learn = true) come first, in Easy then Medium then Hard order, and every one of them is served every time the tool loads. The randomly drawn Learn slots follow. The tool NEVER invents a Learn item while the prop is non empty, and never re-orders the mandatory block.

the tile count, when the question states one
outlineMode, when the side is above 12
question_integration.sceneless_rule: A general claim with no side in it ('why can a square number never be double its side?') has nothing to draw. Render an authored, self consistent case that exhibits the claim, in this tool a side 7 square with its 49 tiles and the doubling answer 14 marked as a short row beside it, rather than fabricating a scene the question does not describe.
question_integration.practice_source: props.questions (delivery_mode = 'Practice'), drawn at random by the platform inside the difficulty and subtype targets. Mandatory checkpoints are never served here.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists so the count is SEEN arriving as seven groups of seven rather than as a block appearing. The array fills a row at a time and the count climbs by a whole row, which is what makes n squared a multiplication instead of an addition. Do not write the rule down at this beat; it is the count that is being made.

Beat 2 is the refutation, and it works because 14 is EXACTLY two rows of seven. The fourteen tiles fill two complete rows and then stop, with five rows of the ruled grid still empty, so the doubling answer is not merely wrong on paper - it is an unfinishable square. The bracket strip then shows 14 sitting between 9 and 16, which is why no whole side gives it at all.

Beat 3 turns the observation into a rule the class can test. The added border arrives as three separately counted pieces and the corner tile lands LAST, so a student who said '+1' watches fifteen tiles land and a student who said '+7' sees the second arm and the corner arrive after their answer was complete. The second chip carries 9 to 10 adding 19, because one step teaches nothing here and two do: the step GROWS, which is precisely why doubling cannot be the rule.
media.generation_prompt: Square Builder: a grid grows from 1 by 1 to 12 by 12 as the student drags a side handle, and the newly added L shaped border shows what each step adds
media.instructions_for_student: 1. Read the side that is set, and type your predicted tile count before anything fills. 2. Fill the square and watch the count climb one row at a time. 3. Compare your prediction with the count that lands beside it. 4. Step the side up by one and name the size of the border that is added. 5. Show the table and read off how the counts grow. 6. Type a rule for any side n and test it; a rule that fails at one value is not a rule. 7. In Practice, answer each item and press Finish when the bank is done.

media.title: What are the areas of squares with these three sides?
media.context: A Square and A Cube. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The video finds the area of squares whose sides are a whole number, a fraction and a decimal, by multiplying the side by itself, and names the perfect square among them. Keeko doubts the area after adding the side to itself.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: the area of a square is its side multiplied by itself, whatever kind of number the side is. A perfect square needs a natural number side. Watch for students who add the side twice instead of multiplying.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

items: Find the areas of squares with sides 6 units, 3/5 unit and 2.5 units.
source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child sees that the area of a square is side times side for every kind of side, and that only a natural number side gives a perfect square.

interaction_points.prompt: What is the area of each square?
covers: Find the areas of squares with sides 6 units, 3/5 unit and 2.5 units.

source: Find the areas of squares with sides 6 units, 3/5 unit and 2.5 units.
video_script.why: The child sees that the area of a square is side times side for every kind of side, and that only a natural number side gives a perfect square.
video_script.substitution: Multiply the side by itself, then check if the side is a natural number.
video_script.anchor: three squares drawn with sides six units, three fifths of a unit and two point five units
video_script.wrong_answer: twelve square units
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko adds six and six to get twelve square units. Twelve unit squares fill only two of the six rows, so the side must be multiplied by itself.
video_script.payoff_line: The areas are thirty six, nine twenty fifths and six point two five square units

final_answer.spoken: thirty six, nine twenty fifths and six point two five square units

never_show: the side lengths of the exercise videos of the topic
maths_rules: area of a square = side × side = side²
6² = 6 × 6 = 36 square units
2.5² = 2.5 × 2.5 = 6.25 square units
perfect squares are the squares of natural numbers: 36 = 6² is one; 9/25 and 6.25 are not, because 3/5 and 2.5 are not natural numbers
the slip: 6 + 6 = 12 adds the side to itself, and 12 unit squares fill only 2 of the 6 rows

media.context: A Square and A Cube. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The video decides which squares end in six by looking only at the last digit of each number. Keeko doubts the answer after thinking only the numbers ending in six give squares ending in six.

source: Which of 38², 34², 46², 56², 74² and 82² end in 6?
video_script.why: The child sees that the units digit of a square is fixed by the units digit of the number, so a quick test is possible without working out the whole square.
video_script.substitution: Square only the last digit of each number and read the last digit of that result.
video_script.anchor: the six numbers thirty eight, thirty four, forty six, fifty six, seventy four and eighty two in a row
video_script.wrong_answer: only the numbers ending in six
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko picks only forty six and fifty six, because they end in six. Numbers ending in four also give a square ending in six, since four times four is sixteen.
video_script.payoff_line: The squares of thirty four, forty six, fifty six and seventy four end in six

final_answer.value: 34², 46², 56² and 74² end in 6; 38² and 82² end in 4
final_answer.spoken: the squares of thirty four, forty six, fifty six and seventy four end in six

never_show: the exercise numbers with 4 in the units place
maths_rules: the units digit of a square depends only on the units digit of the number
38 ends in 8, 8 × 8 = 64, so 38² ends in 4; 82 ends in 2, 2 × 2 = 4, so 82² ends in 4
34 and 74 end in 4, 4 × 4 = 16, so 34² and 74² end in 6
46 and 56 end in 6, 6 × 6 = 36, so 46² and 56² end in 6
the slip: only 46² and 56² is wrong, because 34² and 74² also end in 6

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students find the area of squares of given sides, write the result with the n squared notation, and extend squaring to fractions and decimals.
Students show from the table that squares end only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9, that such an ending does not guarantee a square, and predict the last digit of a square.
Students list squares ending in 1 from numbers ending in 1 or 9 and write numbers ruled out as squares by their units digit alone.

Students predict how many zeros end the square of a number ending in zeros, explain why a square always ends in an even number of zeros, and show that a number and its square are both odd or both even.
Students build squares of tiles of growing side, read the area as the square, and use the last digit, the end zeros and the parity to decide quickly whether a number can be a square.

concepts.concept_name: Odd numbers build squares

content.text:
Perfect Squares and Odd Numbers
Look at the differences between consecutive squares: 4 − 1 = 3, 9 − 4 = 5, 16 − 9 = 7, 25 − 16 = 9. See if this pattern continues.
1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 = 36.
Each square is the previous square with an inverted L shape added to it. The inverted L shapes have 1, 3, 5, 7, ... dots. So the sum of the first n odd numbers is n².
Such pictures are visual proofs.

content.text:
1. Predict first: what is 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11? Guess before you add.
2. Draw a 1 by 1 square of dots, then wrap an inverted L of 3 dots to make 2 by 2, then 5 dots to make 3 by 3.
3. Each new L is the next odd number, so 6 odd numbers make a 6 by 6 square: 36.
4. The sum of the first n odd numbers is n², and consecutive squares differ by consecutive odd numbers.

content.text:
Worked example: Find 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 + 13 + 15 without adding term by term.
1. These are the first 8 odd numbers.
2. The first n odd numbers add up to n².
3. So the sum is 8² = 64.
4. Check: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 + 13 + 15 = 64.
Answer: 64

concepts.concept_name: Subtract odd numbers to test a square

content.text:
Is 25 a perfect square? 25 − 1 = 24, 24 − 3 = 21, 21 − 5 = 16, 16 − 7 = 9, 9 − 9 = 0. We reached 0 after subtracting 5 odd numbers, so 25 = 5².
Is 38 a perfect square? 38 − 1 = 37, 37 − 3 = 34, 34 − 5 = 29, 29 − 7 = 22, 22 − 9 = 13, 13 − 11 = 2, and 2 − 13 is less than 0. So 38 is not a perfect square.

content.text:
1. Predict first: is 38 a perfect square?
2. Subtract the odd numbers in order. If you land exactly on 0, the number is the sum of the first few odd numbers, so it is a square.
3. For 38 we reach 2 and the next odd number, 13, is too big: 38 is not a square.
4. The number of odd numbers subtracted is the square root.

content.text:
Worked example: Use successive subtraction of odd numbers to decide whether 38 is a perfect square.
1. 38 − 1 = 37, 37 − 3 = 34, 34 − 5 = 29.
2. 29 − 7 = 22, 22 − 9 = 13, 13 − 11 = 2.
3. The next odd number is 13 and 2 − 13 = −11, below 0.
4. We never land on 0, so 38 is not a perfect square.
Answer: 38 is not a perfect square

concepts.concept_name: From one square to the next

content.text:
Using the pattern, find 36² given that 35² = 1225.
How do we find the 36th odd number? What is the nth odd number?
The nth odd number is 2n − 1. The 36th odd number is 71. So 36² = 1225 + 71 = 1296.

1. Predict first: if 35² = 1225, is 36² closer to 1260 or to 1300?

3. The odd numbers are 1, 3, 5, ..., and the nth one is 2n − 1, so the 36th is 2 × 36 − 1 = 71.
4. 36² = 1225 + 71 = 1296.

Worked example: Given 35² = 1225, find 36² without multiplying.
1. 36² is the sum of the first 36 odd numbers, which is 35² plus the 36th odd number.
2. The nth odd number is 2n − 1, so the 36th is 2 × 36 − 1 = 71.
3. 36² = 1225 + 71 = 1296.
4. Check: 36 × 36 = 1296.
Answer: 36² = 1296

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students find the differences between consecutive squares, recognise them as the odd numbers, and explain with the inverted L picture why the first n odd numbers add to n squared.
Students subtract 1, 3, 5 and so on from a number in turn and decide it is a perfect square exactly when the subtractions reach 0, counting the steps to find the root.
Students find the nth odd number as 2n − 1 and use it to get the next square from a given square.
Students use the odd number pattern to get squares from neighbouring squares and to check number patterns built from squares.

concepts.concept_name: Square Numbers, Q8

content.text:
Figure it Out (square numbers, question 8): Look at the pattern 1² + 2² + 2² = 3², 2² + 3² + 6² = 7², 3² + 4² + 12² = 13². Fill in 4² + 5² + 20² = (___)² and 9² + 10² + (___)² = (___)².
1. In each line the third number is the product of the first two: 1 × 2 = 2, 2 × 3 = 6, 3 × 4 = 12.
2. The number on the right is one more than that product: 3, 7, 13.
3. 4 × 5 = 20, so 4² + 5² + 20² = 21². Check: 16 + 25 + 400 = 441 = 21².
4. 9 × 10 = 90, so 9² + 10² + 90² = 91². Check: 81 + 100 + 8100 = 8281 = 91².
Answer: 4² + 5² + 20² = 21² and 9² + 10² + 90² = 91²

concepts.concept_name: How many numbers lie between two squares

content.text:
Find how many numbers lie between two consecutive perfect squares. Do you notice a pattern?
Between 1 and 4 lie 2 numbers, between 4 and 9 lie 4 numbers, between 9 and 16 lie 6 numbers.

lines: Find how many numbers lie between two consecutive perfect squares. Do you notice a pattern?

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many whole numbers lie strictly between 25 and 36?
2. The gap from n² to (n + 1)² is the odd number 2n + 1, and the numbers strictly between are one fewer.
3. So there are 2n numbers between n² and (n + 1)²: 10 between 25 and 36.
4. In general, the count between p and q is q − p − 1.

content.text:
Worked example: How many whole numbers lie strictly between 25 and 36?
1. 25 = 5² and 36 = 6² are consecutive squares.
2. The numbers between them are 26 to 35.
3. That is 36 − 25 − 1 = 10 numbers, which is 2 × 5.
Answer: 10 numbers

concepts.concept_name: Squares thin out in each hundred

content.text:
How many square numbers are there between 1 and 100? How many are there between 101 and 200? Write your answers in the table: 1 to 100, 101 to 200, and so on up to 901 to 1000.
What is the largest square less than 1000?

What is the largest square less than 1000?

content.text:
1. Predict first: are there more squares between 1 and 100 or between 901 and 1000?
2. List them: 1 to 100 has 10 squares, 101 to 200 has 4 (121, 144, 169, 196), 201 to 300 has 3.
3. 301 to 400 has 3, then each block from 401 to 900 has 2, and 901 to 1000 has only 961.
4. The gaps 2n + 1 keep growing, so squares get rarer. The largest square below 1000 is 31² = 961, because 32² = 1024.

content.text:
Worked example: How many perfect squares lie between 101 and 200, and what is the largest square less than 1000?
1. 10² = 100 is just below 101 and 15² = 225 is above 200.
2. So the squares are 11² = 121, 12² = 144, 13² = 169 and 14² = 196: 4 squares.
3. 31² = 961 and 32² = 1024, so 961 is the largest square below 1000.
Answer: 4 squares; the largest square below 1000 is 961

video_script.why: The child sees that the numbers between two squares next to each other are counted by subtracting and then leaving out the end number.

Students count the perfect squares in each block of 100 numbers up to 1000, explain why the count drops, and find the largest square below 1000.
Students list the triangular numbers, add consecutive pairs, and explain with a dot picture why each sum is a perfect square.
Students count the numbers between consecutive squares for large squares using 2n instead of listing.

concepts.concept_name: The side of a square from its area

content.text:
Square Roots
The area of a square is 49 sq cm. What is the length of its side? It is 7 cm, because 7² = 49.
If y = x², then x is a square root of y.
What is the square root of 64? Both 8² = 64 and (−8)² = 64, so 64 has two square roots, 8 and −8. Similarly the square roots of 100 are 10 and −10.
In this chapter we will only consider the positive square root, written with the symbol √.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a square has area 64 square cm. Is its side 32 cm, 16 cm or 8 cm?
2. The side times itself must give 64, and 8 × 8 = 64, so the side is 8 cm. Halving gives 32, which is wrong.
3. Finding a square root undoes squaring. But (−8)² = 64 as well, so 64 has two square roots, 8 and −8.
4. A length cannot be negative, so for sides and in this chapter we use the positive root: √64 = 8.

content.text:
Worked example: A square has area 64 square cm. Find its side, and give both square roots of 64.
1. The side s satisfies s × s = 64.
2. 8 × 8 = 64, so the side is 8 cm.
3. Also (−8)² = −8 × −8 = 64, so the square roots of 64 are 8 and −8.
4. A side is a length, so it is the positive root, 8 cm.
Answer: The side is 8 cm; the square roots of 64 are 8 and −8

concepts.concept_name: Find a root by listing squares

content.text:
Is 576 a perfect square? Is 327? How can we find their square roots?
Squares end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9, so 327, which ends in 7, is not a perfect square.
Method 1: list the squares near it. 20² = 400, 21² = 441, 22² = 484, 23² = 529, 24² = 576. So √576 = 24.

content.text:
1. Predict first: which of 576 and 327 could be a perfect square?
2. 327 ends in 7, and no square ends in 7, so 327 is out.
3. For 576: 20² = 400 is too small and 30² = 900 too big, so the root is in the twenties.
4. List 21², 22², 23², 24² until you hit 576: √576 = 24.

content.text:
Worked example: Decide whether 576 and 327 are perfect squares, and find the square root of the one that is.
1. 327 ends in 7, and no square ends in 7, so 327 is not a perfect square.
2. 20² = 400 and 30² = 900, so the root of 576 is between 20 and 30.
3. 21² = 441, 22² = 484, 23² = 529, 24² = 576.
4. So 576 is a perfect square and √576 = 24.
Answer: Only 576 is a perfect square, and √576 = 24

concepts.concept_name: Find a root by subtracting odd numbers

content.text:
Method 2: successive subtraction of odd numbers. 81 − 1 = 80, 80 − 3 = 77, 77 − 5 = 72, 72 − 7 = 65, 65 − 9 = 56, 56 − 11 = 45, 45 − 13 = 32, 32 − 15 = 17, 17 − 17 = 0. We subtracted 9 odd numbers, so √81 = 9.
Finding √729 this way would take a long time.

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many odd numbers must you subtract from 81 to reach 0?
2. 81 is the sum of the first few odd numbers; the count of those odd numbers is the root.
3. Subtract 1, 3, 5, ... and count: 9 steps reach 0, so √81 = 9.
4. For a big number like 729 this needs 27 steps, so a faster method is needed.

concepts.concept_name: Practice: find the side from the area

content.text:
The side of a square is the positive square root of its area.
A square root is not half the number.
List squares near the number, or subtract odd numbers, to find a root.

content.text:
Figure it Out (square numbers, question 4): What is the length of the side of a square whose area is 441 m²?
1. The side is √441.
2. 20² = 400 and 30² = 900, so the side is between 20 and 30.
3. 441 ends in 1, so the root ends in 1 or 9: 21 or 29.
4. 21² = 441, so the side is 21 m.
Answer: 21 m

media.title: Root As Side Length
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash Chapter 1 'A Square and A Cube', the square-root section. The class has built squares forwards and now has to run the same picture backwards, from the area to the side. Squaring, perfect squares and prime factorisation are assumed; the criterion vocabulary of estimation between consecutive squares is NOT - it is introduced here and is built from two multiplications every time it appears. Positive root only: this is the geometric reading and a side of minus eight is not a length, so no negative root is ever drawn or named. The words irrational, surd, non-terminating and approximation are not used, because this class has not met them.

The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the square and number line that explain it.

overview.goal: The student finds the side length of a square given its area, rejects halving as a method, and says that a non perfect area still has a side but not a whole number one.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground with one square above a number line, the way a figure sits over a ruler. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class says the side of a square of area 64 is 32, and the number line is asked to separate the two answers.
overview.concept: The square root of a number a is the side length of a square whose area is a. Halving gives a different number entirely, and the two only ever coincide at a equal to 4. When a is not a perfect square the side still exists, it simply is not a whole number, and it lies between the two nearest whole sides.
overview.purpose: The student finds the side length of a square given its area, rejects halving as a method, and says that a non perfect area still has a side but not a whole number one.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Square fills the upper main panel, number line directly beneath it at full width, readouts to the right on a wide frame and collapsed into one strip under the line on a 390 px frame. The two markers are never drawn closer than 60 px apart; the line rescales instead. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not place the true side marker on the number line while a prediction is still open. The marker IS the answer.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.

titleFraming.normal: Free Play · Root As Side Length

overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Area is side times side, so recovering the side means undoing a multiplication by the same number, not undoing a doubling. Halving inverts adding a number to itself; rooting inverts multiplying a number by itself. The number line makes the difference concrete: at area 64 the half marker sits at 32 while the true side sits at 8, and the gap between them widens as the area grows. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): The halving method has exactly one success, and it is a coincidence. Breaks: The square root taken as half the number, which survives because area 4 keeps confirming it. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): Halving already fails at the smallest square there is. Breaks: The square root taken as half the number. ML3 (Medium, Edge Case): The tool must refuse to draw rather than round a side to make the picture work. Breaks: Believing every area has a whole number side. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): The halving error does not stay small, it grows with the area. Breaks: Treating root as half as a rough estimate rather than as wrong. ML5 (Hard, Conceptual): Not a whole number is a different statement from no answer. Breaks: Believing that if there is no whole answer then there is no answer.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on a square of area 64 with the side hidden and the line empty, and ask the class to commit closer to 8 or closer to 32, out loud. Commit the class answer. media.description: One square stands on a countable unit grid above one number line of side lengths, the way a figure sits over a ruler. The square carries the area it really has printed inside it; the grid inside it is drawn at whole units so the side can be counted rather than guessed, and the unit is derived once per panel and then held constant across every area and every mode, so a bigger side is visibly bigger instead of being rescaled to fill the frame. Beneath, the number line runs from a drawn and labelled zero with arrowheads at both ends, ticks generated from the domain, and an italic caption reading side length. Two markers live on that one line at that one origin: the true side in the accent, with a pulsing dot and its value above the line, and the halving claim in the second accent, hollow and dashed, with its value and the words halving claims below the line - the claim is labelled as a claim about a LENGTH, never as half an area, so the tool does not model the very confusion of quantity it exists to break. When the area is a perfect square the handle settles on the whole side and the square fills green, which is the terminal moment of the search. When it is not, the tool refuses to snap and refuses to round: the square stays drawn at full strength, a shaded band appears between the two neighbouring whole sides with each end named, and the side is shown to three decimals with a trailing ellipsis and the plain statement that the digits go on and on. Beside the figure a two-line working strip prints the chapter's own line of working - the multiplication, then the drawn radical - and for a non-perfect area it prints the two multiplications that bracket it, so the bracket is built on screen rather than assumed as vocabulary the class has not met. The halving misconception is killed by construction rather than by assertion: the claimed side of 32 is drawn as its own dashed square of 1024 square units that runs clean off the top of the board.

concept.notation: Write the square root of a as root a. The root of a is the side of a square whose area is a, not half of a.
concept.statement: The square root of a number a is the side length of a square whose area is a. Halving gives a different number entirely, and the two only ever coincide at a equal to 4. When a is not a perfect square the side still exists, it simply is not a whole number, and it lies between the two nearest whole sides.
prerequisites: area of a square as side times side
misconceptions: Square root estimated as half of the number, so root 64 is taken as 32.
Believing a non perfect area has no side at all, rather than a side that is not whole.
concept.why_it_is_true: Area is side times side, so recovering the side means undoing a multiplication by the same number, not undoing a doubling. Halving inverts adding a number to itself; rooting inverts multiplying a number by itself. The number line makes the difference concrete: at area 64 the half marker sits at 32 while the true side sits at 8, and the gap between them widens as the area grows.
worked_numbers: Area 64: the side is 8, while half the area is 32, which is four times too big.
Area 40: no whole side works, and the side lies between 6 and 7 because 36 is 40 and 49 is not.
Area 4: the side is 2 and half the area is also 2, which is the single case where halving accidentally agrees.

answer_key.worked: The square root of an area is the side of the square that has that area. Halving the area gives a different number, and only area 4 makes the two agree.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn square: the exact side when the area is a perfect square, otherwise the pair of whole sides the true side lies between.
answer_key.precision: The side is held as a rational drag value and areas are compared with a tolerance of 0.001, but every graded value comes from exact integer work. A non integral root is shown to three decimals with a trailing ellipsis and the tool never claims the decimal ends.
answer_key.ground_truth: exactSide(a) = the integer s with s*s === a, found by integer search, or null. boundingPair(a) = [floor, floor+1] where floor is the largest integer f with f*f <= a, found by integer search. halfMarker(a) = a / 2, drawn only as the contrast marker and never graded as an answer.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The true side and the half marker land on the same point, which is the one case where halving is accidentally right. The tool says so plainly rather than hiding the case, because a rule that fails everywhere except one point is worth meeting.

The handle does not snap and the square does not turn green. The tool states that there is no whole number side and shows the nearest two whole sides, and it never rounds the side to make the picture close.
The side is 1 and the square is a single tile. Half the area is 0.5, which is drawn on the line below the smallest legal side, so the halving answer is not even a possible side.
Blocked before the operation with a stated reason on screen. A square of zero area is degenerate and a negative area is not a region, so the tool refuses rather than rendering a zero area figure.

edge_cases.case: A side dragged past the drawn range
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The drag clamps at 20 and the area readout stops with it. The tool says the handle has reached the end of the board rather than silently continuing to compute off screen.

constraints: The area readout always equals side times side to the shown precision, so the figure and the number can never disagree on screen.
The figure stays a square while the handle is dragged; the two sides are one value and cannot be separated.
Whether an area is a perfect square is decided by integer search, never by rounding a floating point root, so exact squares do not fall to the wrong side.
A non integral root is displayed to three decimals with a trailing ellipsis and an explicit approximation marker. The tool never states or implies that the expansion terminates.
Area 0 and negative areas are blocked before the operation with the reason on screen; no zero area figure is ever rendered as a result.

No whole side: the area is set to 40, the handle refuses to snap, and the two whole sides 6 and 7 are named as the pair the true side lies between.

learn.fallback: If props.learnQuestions arrives empty, fall back to the authored set: area 64, area 40, area 4, area 144, and the question of whether a square of area 40 has a side at all.
learn.done_when: The last Learn item has been revealed. No Finish button renders in Learn.
learn.driven_by: The teaching agent, through next() / prev(); the on screen Prev / Next also work for a reviewer.
learn.opens_with: The first mandatory checkpoint from props.learnQuestions, its square already built from the question's own area.

normal.shows: The square, the number line, every control, no score and no question.
steps: No steps. Nothing is mandatory and nothing is scored.
normal.done_when: The student presses Finish, which emits finished once.
normal.opens_with: A square of area 64 with the handle free, snapping on, and both markers live.
play_modes: HALVING HUNT: find every area from 1 to 400 where halving gives the true side, then say why the list is one long.
NO WHOLE SIDE: find three areas between 30 and 60 with no whole side and name the pair each falls between.
GROWING ERROR: pick two areas and show that the halving error grows as the area grows.
MAKE YOUR OWN: set any area in range, predict the side, then drag to check it.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example setting an area a child offers and letting the class watch whether the handle snaps.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

practice.selection: Six served per load, one drawn at random from each slot's five item type. Composition is fixed and the specific question inside a slot is random, so repeat visits to the same tool show different questions.
practice.exclusions: Nothing shown solved in Learn is ever served here, checkpoints included. No question text repeats inside this mount. Practice values differ from the textbook's own printed problem values.
practice.source_prop: props.questions, drawn at random inside each slot's difficulty and subtype
practice.interaction_rules: At least 4 distinct interactions, none above 40 per cent, at least 2 per difficulty band, at most 4 the same inside one type of five.
practice.fallback_precedence: DIFFICULTY is fixed and never traded: a Hard slot serves a Hard question or nothing. SUBTYPE gives way second, because it decides what thinking the slot does. SOURCE gives way first, because provenance matters less than the kind of thinking.

visual_behaviour.never: Do not place the true side marker on the number line while a prediction is still open. The marker IS the answer.
visual_behaviour.scene: A square with its area printed inside it and one drag handle on the corner. A number line runs beneath from 0 to the area, carrying a marker at half the area in a neutral tone and a marker at the true side in the primary accent. A green fill marks the moment the area readout matches the target exactly.
visual_behaviour.layout: Square fills the upper main panel, number line directly beneath it at full width, readouts to the right on a wide frame and collapsed into one strip under the line on a 390 px frame. The two markers are never drawn closer than 60 px apart; the line rescales instead.
readouts: Target area and current area, always on screen
Current side, live, to three decimals with an ellipsis when it is not whole
The two whole sides the true side lies between, whenever there is no whole side
animations: Handle drag: the square resizes continuously and the area readout counts with it, so area is felt as a consequence of the side rather than an independent number.
Snap and confirm: on a perfect square the handle settles over 160 ms and the square fills green once, which is the terminal moment of the search.
Marker separation: the half marker and the true side marker travel apart as the area is raised, and the growing gap is drawn as a labelled span rather than left to be noticed.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: The square is scaled to the panel so a side of 20 still fits with its area label legible inside; the number line rescales so the two markers stay at least 60 px apart on a 390 px frame.

teaching_sequence.rationale: Halving has to be seen failing on the line beside the true side, or root as half is corrected by assertion and returns the next lesson

tool_config.image_prompts_note: Empty by design. This mount is a mechanism, not a depiction, and the standard mandates hand-built inline SVG with no external asset dependency, so no depictive picture is declared.
mathematical_facts: The side of a square of area A is the number s with s times s equal to A
Halving the area gives the side only for area 4, and for no other area from 1 to 400
An area that is not a perfect square still has a side; it is simply not a whole number

question_integration.test: Freeze any injected step and ask: could the teacher read every number in this question off THIS screen? If not, fix the scene, not the words.
question_integration.parse_rule: Read the area out of the question text (the first integer described as an area, a number of tiles or a square measure) and set targetArea to it. If the question names a side instead, read that and set targetArea to its square. The square drawn must carry every number the question mentions.
question_integration.compute_rule: Build the scene from the parsed numbers, then compute the answer with the tool's own ground truth function ON THE DRAWN SCENE. Never carry the bank's answer as truth while drawing a different scene. The two must agree by construction; if they disagree the scene is wrong, not the bank.
question_integration.learn_source: props.learnQuestions (delivery_mode = 'Learn'). Mandatory checkpoints (stickers.mandatory_learn = true) come first, in Easy then Medium then Hard order, and every one of them is served every time the tool loads. The randomly drawn Learn slots follow. The tool NEVER invents a Learn item while the prop is non empty, and never re-orders the mandatory block.
scene_fields: targetArea, the area printed inside the square
side, when the question states one
snapToWhole, off when the question is about a non perfect area
question_integration.sceneless_rule: A general claim with no area in it ('why is the square root of a number not half of it?') has nothing to drag. Render an authored, self consistent case that exhibits the claim, in this tool the area 64 square with both markers on the line at 8 and at 32, rather than fabricating a scene the question does not describe.
question_integration.practice_source: props.questions (delivery_mode = 'Practice'), drawn at random by the platform inside the difficulty and subtype targets. Mandatory checkpoints are never served here.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 is the whole idea in one picture, and it is worth slowing down on the GRID rather than the number. The square of area 64 is drawn eight units on a side with eight columns and eight rows on screen, so a child can count the side instead of accepting it. Say the chapter's own line out loud as the strip prints it: area is side times side, so eight times eight is sixty-four, so the side is the square root of sixty-four. Ask the class to commit, out loud, whether the side is closer to 8 or to 32 BEFORE you land the beat, and commit their answer with predict('closer to 8') or predict('closer to 32'). The prediction is spoken; nothing on the screen asks for it.

Beat 2 is the argument, and the argument is a picture, not a sentence. Do not say halving is wrong and move on: point at the dashed square that the halving claim builds. A side of 32 draws a square of 1024 square units that does not fit on the board at all, beside a square of 64 that does. Then point at the two markers sitting on ONE line from ONE zero - 8 in the accent, 32 in the warm colour - and say that the second number is not a rough version of the first, it is a different number produced by a different rule. Halving undoes adding a number to itself; rooting undoes multiplying a number by itself.

Beat 3 is where the class will offer 6.5, and that is the moment to use. Six and a half times six and a half is 42.25, which overshoots 40, so the true side sits BELOW the midpoint of the bracket - the marker on screen is at 6.325 and you can see it sitting left of centre in the shaded band. Insist on the two statements being different: there is no WHOLE side, and there IS a side. The square of area 40 is drawn at full strength while the handle refuses to snap, precisely so refusing to snap cannot be read as refusing to exist. Say the ending in this grade's words - the digits go on and on and never stop - and do not reach for the word irrational.
media.generation_prompt: Root As Side Length: a square with its area printed inside and a number line below carrying two markers, one at half the area and one at the true side, so halving is visibly wrong
media.instructions_for_student: 1. Read the area printed inside the square and predict whether the side is near its half or far from it. 2. Set the side until the area readout matches the target. 3. Compare the true side marker with the half marker on the line. 4. Try an area that is not a perfect square and watch the handle refuse to snap. 5. Name the two whole numbers the side falls between. 6. In Practice, answer each item and press Finish when the bank is done.

media.title: What is the side of this square, and the roots of sixty four?

media.description: The video finds the side of a square from its area of sixty four square centimetres, and gives both square roots of sixty four. Keeko doubts the roots after saying sixty four has only one, forgetting that a negative number squared is also positive.

media.title: How do we find the square root of 81 by taking away odd numbers?
media.context: A Square and A Cube. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The video finds the square root of eighty one by taking away odd numbers from one onwards until nothing is left, then counting them. Keeko doubts the root after naming the last odd number taken away instead of counting them.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: take away odd numbers from one onwards until the leftover is exactly zero, and the count of odd numbers taken away is the square root. Watch for students who give the last odd number instead of the count.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How do we find the square root of 81 by taking away odd numbers?
items: Find √81 by successive subtraction of odd numbers.
source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child learns that taking away odd numbers one after another from a perfect square ends at zero, and that the number of odd numbers taken away is its square root.

interaction_points.prompt: What is the square root of eighty one?
covers: Find √81 by successive subtraction of odd numbers.

source: Find √81 by successive subtraction of odd numbers.
video_script.why: The child learns that taking away odd numbers one after another from a perfect square ends at zero, and that the number of odd numbers taken away is its square root.
video_script.substitution: Take away 1, 3, 5 and so on until the leftover is zero, then count how many odd numbers were taken away.
video_script.anchor: the number eighty one with the odd numbers one, three, five and so on lined up beside it
video_script.wrong_answer: the square root is seventeen
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko names the last odd number taken away, 17, as the square root. 17 is only the last odd number; the root is how many odd numbers were taken away, which is 9.
video_script.payoff_line: The square root of eighty one is nine

final_answer.spoken: the square root of eighty one is nine

concepts.concept_name: Two equal groups of prime factors

content.text:
Method 3: prime factorisation.
Is 324 a perfect square? 324 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3. The prime factors can be split into two equal groups, 2 × 3 × 3 and 2 × 3 × 3. So 324 = (2 × 3 × 3)² = 18², and √324 = 18.
Is 156 a perfect square? 156 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 13. The factors 3 and 13 cannot be paired, so 156 is not a perfect square.

1. Predict first: is 324 a perfect square? It ends in 4, so it might be.

3. Split into two equal groups, 2 × 3 × 3 each, so 324 = 18 × 18 and √324 = 18.
4. For 156 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 13, the 3 and the 13 have no partner, so 156 is not a square. Having one repeated prime is not enough.
