content.text:
Worked example: Use prime factorisation to decide whether 324 and 156 are perfect squares.
1. 324 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3.
2. The primes split into two equal groups: (2 × 3 × 3) × (2 × 3 × 3) = 18 × 18 = 324.
3. 156 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 13; the 3 and the 13 cannot be paired.
4. So 324 = 18² is a perfect square and 156 is not.
Answer: 324 is a perfect square with √324 = 18; 156 is not a perfect square

content.text:
Worked example: Using prime factorisation, find whether 1156 and 2800 are perfect squares.
1. 1156 = 2 × 2 × 17 × 17, so it splits as (2 × 17) × (2 × 17) = 34 × 34.
2. So 1156 = 34², a perfect square.
3. 2800 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 × 5 × 7; the single 7 has no partner.
4. So 2800 is not a perfect square, even though it ends in two zeros.
Answer: 1156 = 34² is a perfect square; 2800 is not

concepts.concept_name: Practice: pair the prime factors

content.text:
A perfect square has every prime factor appearing an even number of times.
One group of the pairs, multiplied out, is the square root.
Multiplying by the unpaired primes makes the smallest perfect square multiple.
content.publication_text:

content.text:
Figure it Out (square numbers, question 5): Find the smallest square number that is divisible by each of the following numbers: 4, 9 and 10.
1. The number must be a multiple of 4 = 2 × 2, 9 = 3 × 3 and 10 = 2 × 5.
2. The smallest such multiple is 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 = 180.
3. In 180 the 5 has no partner, so multiply by 5: 180 × 5 = 900.
4. 900 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 5 = 30², and it is divisible by 4, 9 and 10.
Answer: 900

media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash Chapter 1 'A Square and A Cube', square roots by prime factorisation. It follows the root as a side length: the student can already find a root by searching and now needs a method that says, without searching, whether a root exists at all. overview.goal: The student decides whether a number is a perfect square by pairing its prime factors, and states the smallest multiplier that makes it one.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground with a loose rail of prime factor tiles above a rebuild area. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A number is claimed not to be a perfect square, and the class is asked to say exactly what is stopping it.
overview.concept: A number is a perfect square exactly when every prime in its factorisation appears an even number of times, because the tiles can then be split into two identical halves and each half is the square root. A prime with an odd exponent leaves one tile unpaired, and the smallest multiplier that fixes it is the product of exactly those unpaired primes.
overview.purpose: The student decides whether a number is a perfect square by pairing its prime factors, and states the smallest multiplier that makes it one.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Tile rail fills the main panel with the verdict strip beneath it and the multiply box under that. The factor tree, when shown, sits to the right on a wide frame and collapses above the rail on a 390 px frame. Draggable tiles are never placed closer than 60 px apart. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the verdict, the root or the smallest multiplier while a prediction is still open. The leftover tile IS the answer.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. If every prime appears an even number of times, the tiles split into two identical groups whose product is the same number s, so the original is s times s. If some prime appears an odd number of times, no such split exists, because one group would have to hold more copies of that prime than the other. The multiplier that repairs it must supply exactly one more copy of each odd prime, and nothing else, which is why it is the smallest. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with 180 broken into prime tiles, unpaired, and asks the class to decide whether it is a perfect square before anything is moved. Beat 2 pairs what pairs and leaves the single leftover tile red, so the obstruction is one visible object. Beat 3 multiplies by that leftover, rebuilds the factorisation, and the new number pairs completely. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setNumber, autoPair, multiplyBy and say. No drag: the agent cannot drag a tile with finite calls.

The smallest multiplier is the product of the odd exponent primes
The smallest divisor that gives a square is that same number
conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on 180 shown as loose prime tiles with nothing paired and no verdict, and ask the class to commit square or not a square, out loud. Commit the class verdict. Target the number 180. Never pair a tile before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Pair everything that pairs and leave the single 5 red and alone, then point at it. Targets the two 2s, the two 3s, and the lone 5. Read the factorisation from the tool's own tray. Call 3. Multiply by 5, let the factorisation rebuild, and read the root off one tile from each pair. Targets the multiplier 5, the rebuilt 900, and the root 30.

hunts: ONE TILE SHORT: find three numbers under 200 that need exactly one extra prime.
SAME NUMBER TWICE: find a number whose smallest multiplier equals its smallest divisor, then say why that always happens.
ALREADY SQUARE: find the smallest number above 100 that needs no multiplier at all.
MAKE YOUR OWN: type any number in range, pair its tiles, then predict its multiplier before the tool shows it.

media.description: A number breaks into prime tiles on a loose rail, one tile per copy of each prime, drawn smallest prime first the way the Class 8 division ladder produces them. Two identical tiles lock together into a single green capsule; two unlike tiles refuse to join, shake apart and say why, so the rule is learnt from the refusal rather than from a red cross. A tile with no partner left anywhere stays outlined in red, which makes the obstruction one object the class can point at instead of a feeling that the number looks wrong. Above the rail the factorisation is typeset with real exponents, and beneath it, whenever every tile pairs, the two equal groups NCERT actually prints are written out as (2 × 3 × 5) × (2 × 3 × 5) with the root read off one of them. Multiplying rebuilds the factorisation as a fresh rail underneath the first, so a multiplier that only repairs half the problem visibly leaves a tile still red. A division ladder can be opened beside the rail. Concept walks 180 in three beats, Learn works the five reviewed checkpoints already answered, Practice serves six drawn questions on a difficulty ladder with a review pass, and Free Play unlocks the number box, the multiply box and free pairing with nothing scored.

concept.notation: Write the factorisation as a product of primes with exponents, for example 180 as 2 squared times 3 squared times 5. An exponent counts how many copies of that prime the number holds.
concept.statement: A number is a perfect square exactly when every prime in its factorisation appears an even number of times, because the tiles can then be split into two identical halves and each half is the square root. A prime with an odd exponent leaves one tile unpaired, and the smallest multiplier that fixes it is the product of exactly those unpaired primes.
prerequisites: prime factorisation and factor trees from Class 7
square numbers as n times n
misconceptions: Perfect square judged by appearance or by size rather than by the structure of its factors.
Square root treated as an operation with no factor meaning, so the pairing is copied as a procedure without the exponent link.
concept.why_it_is_true: If every prime appears an even number of times, the tiles split into two identical groups whose product is the same number s, so the original is s times s. If some prime appears an odd number of times, no such split exists, because one group would have to hold more copies of that prime than the other. The multiplier that repairs it must supply exactly one more copy of each odd prime, and nothing else, which is why it is the smallest.
worked_numbers: 180 is 2 squared times 3 squared times 5: the 5 is alone, so 180 is not a square and multiplying by 5 gives 900, which is 30 squared.
1225 is 5 squared times 7 squared: everything pairs, so it is a square and its root is 5 times 7, that is 35.
72 is 2 cubed times 3 squared: one 2 is alone, so multiplying by 2 gives 144, which is 12 squared.

answer_key.worked: A number is a perfect square exactly when every prime appears an even number of times. The smallest multiplier that makes it one is the product of the primes with odd exponents.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn tile set: whether every exponent is even, the root read off as one tile from each pair, or the product of the odd exponent primes.
answer_key.precision: Integer arithmetic only, with factorisation by trial division up to the integer square root. Exponents are held as a map from prime to count, never inferred from a decimal.
answer_key.ground_truth: factorise(k) = trial division by d from 2 while d*d <= k, returning a Map from prime to exponent. isSquare(k) = every exponent in factorise(k) is even. root(k) = product of p to the power e/2 over the map, computed only when isSquare(k). smallestMultiplier(k) = product of every prime whose exponent is odd.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The tile set is empty and every exponent is vacuously even, so 1 is a perfect square with root 1. The tool says so rather than treating an empty set as an error.

One tile, always unpaired, so it is never a square and the smallest multiplier is the prime itself. Worth showing because students expect primes to behave specially and here they behave in the simplest possible way.
The multiplier is the product of both, not either one alone. The tool refuses a multiplier that only fixes half the problem and shows which tile is still red.

edge_cases.case: A number that is already a perfect square
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The smallest multiplier is 1. The tool states that explicitly rather than leaving the box empty, because 1 is an answer and not an absence.
Blocked before factorising, with the cap of 10 to the power 6 and its reason stated on screen, so the trial division stays instant on a phone.

constraints: The multiset of prime tiles always multiplies back to the original number. A pairing move can never change the product, and a move that would is refused with the reason on screen.
Factorisation is by trial division up to the integer square root, with exponents stored as a map from prime to count.
The number is capped at 10 to the power 6 and the cap and its reason are stated on screen, so factorisation stays instant.
A pair may only contain two identical primes. A drag that would pair unlike tiles is refused and the tiles separate rather than being silently corrected.
The square root is announced only as the product of one tile from each pair, never computed by a floating point root, so the method and the answer stay the same object.

steps: Predict: 180 is shown as loose prime tiles with nothing paired and no verdict. The class commits square or not a square out loud and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Pair: everything that pairs locks green and the single 5 is left red and alone, so the obstruction is one object rather than a feeling.
Repair: multiplying by 5 rebuilds the factorisation as 900, every tile pairs, and the root 30 is read off as one tile from each pair.

practice.shows: The item's own tile set, the question, the answer affordance, a running score, and the Finish button.
steps: One item at a time from props.questions; the tool never re-orders or filters the bank.
practice.review: The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the pairing that explains it.

interactions.response: The pair splits back into two loose tiles.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example factorising a number a child names and letting the class see which tile is left over.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

steps: Both are the product of the primes with an odd exponent, because that product is what stops the exponents being even.
Take 180, whose odd exponent product is 5.
180 times 5 is 900, which is 30 squared.
180 divided by 5 is 36, which is 6 squared.
Now take 2400, whose odd exponent product is 6.
2400 times 6 is 14400, which is 120 squared.
2400 divided by 6 is 400, which is 20 squared.
items.answer: No: they are always the same number, the product of the odd exponent primes
items.method: Compare the smallest multiplier with the smallest divisor

items.checkpoint: One structural fact answers two questions that look opposite.
items.misconception: Believing multiplying up and dividing down are unrelated repairs.

visual_behaviour.never: Do not show the verdict, the root or the smallest multiplier while a prediction is still open. The leftover tile IS the answer.
visual_behaviour.scene: Prime factor tiles laid out on a loose rail, each carrying its prime. A paired tile locks to its partner as a single green capsule; an unpaired tile stays outlined in the warning tone. A rebuilt factorisation after a multiply drops in as a fresh rail beneath the old one so the two can be compared.
visual_behaviour.layout: Tile rail fills the main panel with the verdict strip beneath it and the multiply box under that. The factor tree, when shown, sits to the right on a wide frame and collapses above the rail on a 390 px frame. Draggable tiles are never placed closer than 60 px apart.
readouts: The number and its factorisation as a product of primes, always on screen
How many tiles are paired and how many are still loose, live
The root, or the smallest multiplier, once the pairing is complete
animations: Pair lock: two identical tiles slide together over 180 ms and fuse into one green capsule, so a pair reads as a single object rather than two adjacent ones.
Refused pair: unlike tiles shake once over 200 ms and spring apart, and the reason is stated, so an illegal move is answered rather than undone.
Rebuild after multiply: the new prime tile drops onto the rail and the whole set relays into pairs, which is the moment the repair becomes visible as a repair.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: Tile size is derived from the panel width and the tile count so every prime stays at least 16 px and every tile keeps a 44 px hit target; above 24 tiles the rail wraps to a second row rather than shrinking the tiles.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The single unpaired tile has to be seen before the even exponent rule is stated, or the rule is a test to apply rather than an obstruction to name

tool_config.image_prompts_note: Empty by design. This mount is a mechanism, not a depiction, and the standard mandates hand-built inline SVG with no external asset dependency, so no depictive picture is declared.

question_integration.test: Freeze any injected step and ask: could the teacher read every number in this question off THIS screen? If not, fix the scene, not the words.
question_integration.parse_rule: Read the number out of the question text (the first integer described as a number, a value or the thing being tested) and set number to it, refusing anything above 10 to the power 6. If the question names a multiplier or a divisor, apply it only after the base factorisation is on screen. The tile set drawn must account for every prime the question mentions.
question_integration.compute_rule: Build the scene from the parsed numbers, then compute the answer with the tool's own ground truth function ON THE DRAWN SCENE. Never carry the bank's answer as truth while drawing a different scene. The two must agree by construction; if they disagree the scene is wrong, not the bank.

Mandatory checkpoints (stickers.mandatory_learn = true) come first, in Easy then Medium then Hard order, and every one of them is served every time the tool loads. The randomly drawn Learn slots follow. The tool NEVER invents a Learn item while the prop is non empty, and never re-orders the mandatory block.
scene_fields: the multiplier, when the question states one
showFactorTree, on when the question refers to the tree
question_integration.sceneless_rule: A general claim with no number in it ('why must every prime appear an even number of times in a perfect square?') has nothing to factorise. Render an authored, self consistent case that exhibits the claim, in this tool 180 with its single red 5 beside 900 with everything paired, rather than fabricating a scene the question does not describe.
question_integration.practice_source: props.questions (delivery_mode = 'Practice'), drawn at random by the platform inside the difficulty and subtype targets. Mandatory checkpoints are never served here.

The class is asked out loud whether 180 is a perfect square while five loose tiles sit on the rail; the single 5 is already outlined in red, which is the evidence, not the verdict. Say the rule once here and let the tiles carry it.

Beat 2 is the argument in one motion. Everything that can pair locks into green capsules and exactly one tile is left alone, so 'not a square' stops being an opinion about how 180 looks and becomes a thing on screen with a colour and a position. Point at the red 5 and let a child name it.

Beat 3 turns the observation into an instrument. Multiplying by that same 5 rebuilds the rail as 900, every tile pairs, and the two equal groups (2 × 3 × 5) and (2 × 3 × 5) are written under it with the root 30 read off one of them, the NCERT justification, not a second trick.

concepts.concept_name: Square Numbers, Q6

content.text:
Figure it Out (square numbers, question 6): Find the smallest number by which 9408 must be multiplied so that the product is a perfect square. Find the square root of the product.
1. 9408 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 × 7.
2. The 2s and the 7s pair up; the single 3 has no partner.
3. Multiply by 3: 9408 × 3 = 28224.
4. 28224 = (2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 7)² = 168².
Answer: Multiply by 3; the product 28224 has square root 168

concepts.concept_name: Square Numbers, Q9

content.text:
Figure it Out (square numbers, question 9): How many tiny squares are there in the picture of 9 rows of 9 tiles, where every tile, upright or turned, is a grid of 5 by 5 tiny squares? Write the prime factorisation of the number of tiny squares.
1. There are 9 × 9 = 81 tiles.
2. Each tile has 5 × 5 = 25 tiny squares.
3. Total: 81 × 25 = 2025.
4. 2025 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 5 = 3⁴ × 5², so the primes pair up and 2025 = 45².
Answer: 2025 tiny squares, and 2025 = 3⁴ × 5², which is 45²

concepts.concept_name: Pin down the root of a perfect square

content.text:
Estimating Square Roots
Find √1936. Since 40² = 1600 and 50² = 2500, the root lies between 40 and 50.
1936 ends in 6, so the root ends in 4 or 6: it is 44 or 46.
45² = 2025, which is more than 1936, so the root is less than 45. So √1936 = 44.

content.text:
1. Predict first: is √1936 nearer 40 or nearer 50?
2. 40² = 1600 and 50² = 2500 trap the root between 40 and 50.
3. Squares ending in 6 come from numbers ending in 4 or 6, so the root is 44 or 46.
4. 45² = 2025 is above 1936, so the root is below 45: √1936 = 44.

content.text:
Worked example: Find √1936 without long multiplication.
1. 40² = 1600 < 1936 < 2500 = 50², so the root is between 40 and 50.
2. 1936 ends in 6, so the root ends in 4 or 6: 44 or 46.
3. 45² = 2025 > 1936, so the root is less than 45.
4. So √1936 = 44. Check: 44 × 44 = 1936.
Answer: √1936 = 44

concepts.concept_name: A root between two whole numbers

content.text:
Aribam and Bijou play a game. One says a number and the other guesses its square root. Aribam says 25, Bijou says 5. Bijou says 81, Aribam says 9. Then Aribam says 250.
250 is not a perfect square. 10² = 100 and 14² = 196 are too small, and 15² = 225 and 16² = 256 trap it: √250 lies between 15 and 16, closer to 16.

content.text:
1. Predict first: Bijou must guess √250. Is it a whole number?
2. 250 ends in a single 0, and squares end in an even number of zeros, so 250 is not a perfect square.
3. 15² = 225 < 250 < 256 = 16², so √250 lies between 15 and 16.
4. 250 is much closer to 256 than to 225, so √250 is a little less than 16.

1. 15² = 225 and 16² = 256.
2. 225 < 250 < 256, so √250 is between 15 and 16.
3. 256 − 250 = 6 while 250 − 225 = 25, so √250 is closer to 16.
Answer: √250 lies between 15 and 16, closer to 16

concepts.concept_name: Akhil's handkerchief

content.text: Akhil has a square piece of cloth of area 125 cm². He wants to make a square handkerchief of side 15 cm. Is it possible? If not, what is the largest whole number side of the handkerchief he can make?

lines: Akhil has a square piece of cloth of area 125 cm². He wants to make a square handkerchief of side 15 cm. Is it possible? If not, what is the largest whole number side of the handkerchief he can make?

content.text:
1. Predict first: can a 15 cm handkerchief come out of a cloth of area 125 cm²?
2. A 15 cm square needs 15² = 225 cm², far more than 125 cm².
3. 11² = 121 ≤ 125 < 144 = 12², so the side of the cloth is between 11 and 12 cm.
4. The largest whole number side is 11 cm.

concepts.concept_name: Practice: trap the root

content.text:
If a² < N < (a + 1)², then √N lies between a and a + 1.
A number whose root is trapped strictly between two whole numbers is not a perfect square.
For a perfect square, the units digit narrows the root to two choices.

content.text:
Figure it Out (square numbers, question 1): Which of the following numbers are not perfect squares? (i) 2032 (ii) 2048 (iii) 1027 (iv) 1089
1. 2032 ends in 2 and 2048 ends in 8, and no square ends in 2 or 8.
2. Also 45² = 2025 and 46² = 2116, so both are trapped strictly between two squares.
3. 32² = 1024 and 33² = 1089, so 1027 is trapped strictly between them; it ends in 7 too.
4. 1089 = 33², a perfect square.
Answer: (i) 2032, (ii) 2048 and (iii) 1027 are not perfect squares; 1089 = 33²

media.title: Root Between Which Numbers
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash chapter 1 'A Square and A Cube' (legacy NCERT chapter 6 'Squares and Square Roots'), the estimating-a-square-root section. It follows the prime-factor pairing tool: the class already knows when a whole root EXISTS and now needs a way to say something exact about the numbers where one does not. The chapter's own three-move procedure is what the tool draws - find the whole number whose square sits just below, state BOTH multiplications, then say which of the two the root is nearer by comparing the number with the two SQUARES. Vocabulary is held at grade: the input is labelled 'Number under the root', never 'radicand', and the words irrational, surd, bound, interval and strictly between appear nowhere on the glass.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the shaded interval with both squarings that explain it.

overview.goal: The student places a non perfect square root between two consecutive whole numbers and names the two multiplications that prove both bounds.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground carrying a single horizontal number line with the perfect squares labelled beneath it. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A root that is not a whole number still has to live somewhere, and the class is asked to say exactly where.
overview.concept: The square root of a number that is not a perfect square still exists and sits between the roots of the two nearest perfect squares. To prove root 55 lies between 7 and 8, both bounds are needed: 7 squared is 49 which is below 55, and 8 squared is 64 which is above it. One squaring alone traps nothing.
overview.purpose: The student places a non perfect square root between two consecutive whole numbers and names the two multiplications that prove both bounds.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: The line runs the full width of the main panel with the flag above it and the labels beneath. Readouts sit to the right on a wide frame and collapse to one strip under the line on a 390 px frame. The line never scrolls; it rescales. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not shade the interval or show either squaring while a prediction is still open. The shading IS the answer.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.

titleFraming.normal: Free Play · Root Between Which Numbers

overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Squaring keeps order for positive numbers: if a is less than b then a squared is less than b squared. So from 49 less than 55 less than 64 it follows that 7 is less than root 55 which is less than 8. The argument runs in both directions at once, which is why both squarings have to be named and not just the nearer one. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the flag off the line and asks the class between which two whole numbers root 55 sits. Beat 2 drops the flag and shades the interval between the two nearest perfect squares. Beat 3 shows both squarings, 7 squared is 49 and 8 squared is 64, so the trap is closed from below and from above rather than asserted. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setRadicand, placeFlag, showBounds and say. No drag: the agent cannot sweep a continuous control with finite calls.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open with the flag off the line and nothing shaded, and ask the class to commit the two whole numbers the root sits between, out loud. Commit the class pair. Target the opening radicand. Never place the flag before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Drop the flag onto the line and shade the interval between the two nearest perfect squares, holding the committed guess beside it. Point at the shading. Read both bounds from the tool's own readouts. Call 3. Show the two multiplications beneath the shading, the square below the radicand and the square above it. Targets the lower square and the upper square. Never state a bound without the multiplication that proves it.

hunts: EXACT HUNT: find every radicand on the line whose root needs no interval at all.
OFF BY ONE: find a radicand one below a perfect square and say which bound it takes.
WIDEST RUN: find the pair of whole bounds that holds the most radicands on this line.
MAKE YOUR OWN: type any radicand in range, place the flag, then let the tool prove both bounds.

media.description: One horizontal number line runs across the frame carrying the ROOTS from 0 to 15, arrowheads at both ends, every whole number labelled beneath it and a flag standing above it. The number being rooted is an AREA, not a position, so it never appears loose under a tick: it is drawn as a typeset radical - a hand-built path with a real overbar - and, once the proof row opens, inside a middle plate that sits between the two multiplications, so the screen reads 7 x 7 = 49 < 55 < 8 x 8 = 64 in one line with a leader drawn from each square up to its own tick. The band between the two whole numbers shades above the line and closes from both sides at once. A zoom rescales the line to that one gap with tenth ticks and swaps the proof row for two bars drawn from ONE origin on ONE unit - 55 minus 49 is 6 against 64 minus 55 is 9 - which is how the class decides which of the two whole numbers the root is nearer without ever being told to halve the gap. Where the number IS a perfect square nothing shades at all: the flag lands on the marker and the tool says the root is whole rather than drawing a band that is not there. Learn walks five reviewed worked examples with the answer already on screen; Practice serves six of thirty reviewed questions on a difficulty ladder, hiding the band and both multiplications until the attempt is in; Free Play unlocks the number, the flag, the squares and the zoom with nothing scored.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the radicand from its own number, shows the question, then reveals the shaded interval, both squarings and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the flag off the line and asks the class between which two whole numbers root 55 sits. Beat 2 drops the flag and shades the interval between the two nearest perfect squares. Beat 3 shows both squarings, 7 squared is 49 and 8 squared is 64, so the trap is closed from below and from above rather than asserted. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setRadicand, placeFlag, showBounds and say. No drag: the agent cannot sweep a continuous control with finite calls.
mods.practice: Practice, student operated. The bank from props.questions, one item at a time, each rendering its own line. Give the bounding pair for a radicand, give a one decimal estimate, or name the two multiplications that prove the bounds. Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer and the interval that settles it.
mods.free_play: Free Play, student operated. The student drags the flag anywhere, types any radicand, zooms into the shaded interval, and shows or hides the perfect square labels. Nothing is scored and nothing is mandatory.

concept.notation: Write root 55 for the square root of 55. Saying it lies between 7 and 8 means 7 is below it and 8 is above it, both strictly.
concept.statement: The square root of a number that is not a perfect square still exists and sits between the roots of the two nearest perfect squares. To prove root 55 lies between 7 and 8, both bounds are needed: 7 squared is 49 which is below 55, and 8 squared is 64 which is above it. One squaring alone traps nothing.
prerequisites: square root as the side of a square of known area
reading and marking a number line
misconceptions: Roots must be whole numbers, so a non perfect radicand is treated as having no root.
Roots of non squares estimated by halving, or by rounding the radicand to the nearest square before rooting.
concept.why_it_is_true: Squaring keeps order for positive numbers: if a is less than b then a squared is less than b squared. So from 49 less than 55 less than 64 it follows that 7 is less than root 55 which is less than 8. The argument runs in both directions at once, which is why both squarings have to be named and not just the nearer one.
worked_numbers: Root 55 lies between 7 and 8, because 7 squared is 49 and 8 squared is 64.
Root 90 lies between 9 and 10, because 9 squared is 81 and 10 squared is 100.
Root 49 is exactly 7, so there is no interval to shade and the tool says so instead of shading a false one.

answer_key.worked: Root 55 lies between 7 and 8, and the proof is the pair 7 squared is 49 and 8 squared is 64. Both squarings are part of the answer.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn line: the bounding pair for the radicand, the one decimal estimate within tolerance, or the two multiplications that prove the bounds.
answer_key.precision: Bounds are found by integer search, never by rounding a floating point root, so exact squares such as 10000 do not fall to the wrong side. A one decimal estimate is graded with a stated tolerance.
answer_key.ground_truth: lower(a) = the largest integer f with f*f <= a, found by integer search. upper(a) = lower(a) + 1 when a is not a perfect square, otherwise lower(a) itself. isExact(a) = lower(a)*lower(a) === a. estimate(a) = the one decimal value nearest root a, graded within a tolerance of 0.05.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A radicand that is a perfect square
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: There is no interval. The flag lands exactly on the labelled marker and the tool states that the root is whole rather than shading a one wide interval around it.
Both are exact and both are drawn. They are legal starting values, not empty cases, and the tool does not skip to the first interesting radicand.

edge_cases.case: A radicand just below a perfect square
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The interval is still the full width between two whole numbers and the flag sits near its top. The tool never narrows the shading to suggest the root is almost whole.

edge_cases.case: A student naming only one bound
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The stage stays open. One squaring traps nothing, so the tool asks for the second multiplication rather than accepting a half proof.
Bounds are found by integer search so the answer stays exact past the point where a floating point root would round the wrong way. The line rescales to the interval rather than the whole range.

hostProps.showModeSelector: false in production for every maths tool. Honour it, defaulting to true (const showSelector = props.showModeSelector ?? true) so the selector still works in preview and review, and disappears live.
hostProps.additionalProps.exampleSeed: A 32 bit int the tool's mulberry32 PRNG consumes directly. The teacher agent builds its own copy of the example set from the SAME seed, so Math.random(), Date.now() or ignoring the seed desynchronises the narration from the screen in every single session.

questions.description: Replaces the built in practice bank. Items are {kind:'bounding_pair', a:number} | {kind:'one_decimal', a:number, tolerance:number} | {kind:'name_squarings', a:number} | {kind:'choice', prompt, options[], correct, explain}.

showSquareLabels.description: Label the perfect squares 1, 4, 9, 16 and so on beneath the line. Turned off in the stage that asks for the bounds without them.

startingRadicand.description: The radicand the line opens on, clamped 0 to 225.

constraints: Bounds are computed by integer search, never by rounding Math.sqrt, so a perfect square never falls to the wrong side of its own bound through floating point.
Once the answer is confirmed the flag cannot leave the interval implied by the correct bounds; a drag out of it is refused with the reason on screen.
A one decimal estimate is displayed with an explicit approximation marker and the tool never claims the expansion terminates.
The shaded interval is always the full span between two consecutive whole numbers, never narrowed towards the true root, because narrowing would give the answer away.
Both squarings are required to close the justification stage; naming one bound leaves the stage open with the missing side named.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: The number line with the perfect square markers, the flag, the teacher caption, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: the line is drawn with the flag OFF it and no shading. The class commits the two whole numbers out loud and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Trap it: the flag drops onto the line and the interval between the two nearest perfect squares shades, with the committed guess held beside it.
Prove it: 7 squared is 49 and 8 squared is 64 appear together beneath the shading, closing the trap from below and from above.
ai.done_when: Beat 3 has been reached and both squarings are on screen. Concept has no Finish button.
ai.driven_by: The teaching agent, through next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) and the component calls.
ai.opens_with: A number line from 0 to 15 with the perfect squares labelled beneath, no flag placed and nothing shaded, the predict pad open on 'Root 55 sits between which two whole numbers?'.

normal.shows: The line, the flag, every control, no score and no question.
steps: No steps. Nothing is mandatory and nothing is scored.
normal.done_when: The student presses Finish, which emits finished once.

play_modes: EXACT HUNT: find every radicand on the line whose root needs no interval at all.
OFF BY ONE: find a radicand one below a perfect square and say which bound it takes.
WIDEST RUN: find the pair of whole bounds that holds the most radicands on this line.
MAKE YOUR OWN: type any radicand in range, place the flag, then let the tool prove both bounds.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example trapping a radicand a child names and showing the two squarings that prove it.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

visual_behaviour.layout: The line runs the full width of the main panel with the flag above it and the labels beneath. Readouts sit to the right on a wide frame and collapse to one strip under the line on a 390 px frame. The line never scrolls; it rescales.

Both squarings once the answer is confirmed, and a one decimal estimate when zoomed, marked as approximate
animations: Flag drop: the flag falls onto the line over 200 ms and the interval shades outward from it, so the trap closes around the estimate rather than appearing beneath it.
Both squarings: 7 squared is 49 slides in from the left and 8 squared is 64 from the right, meeting under the shading, which makes the two sided proof a single visual gesture.

visual_behaviour.scale_rule: The line is scaled so consecutive whole number ticks stay at least 24 px apart on a 390 px frame; when the radicand is large the line rescales to the neighbourhood of the interval rather than compressing the whole range.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the claim before the proof. The flag lands and the band shades, and the only thing on screen besides the line is the number itself, typeset under a radical. The class can already read the answer off the picture - which is exactly the position a student is in when they guess, and it is why beat 2 has something to do.

Beat 2 is the whole argument, and it is a two-sided one. 49 arrives from the left and 64 from the right and the row closes as 49 < 55 < 64, each square joined to its own tick by a drawn leader so nobody reads 49 as a position on a line that only goes to 15. Say the second multiplication out loud even when the class thinks the first settled it: with only 49 named, everything above 7 is still open.

Beat 3 turns the pair into an estimate and kills the halfway misconception in one picture. The line rescales to the one gap and the two bars - 6 against 9 - are drawn from the same origin on the same unit, so the class SEES that 55 sits nearer 49 than 64 and therefore the root sits nearer 7. Compare the number with the two SQUARES, never with the two whole numbers: that is the move students invert.
media.generation_prompt: Root Between Which Numbers: a number line from 0 to 15 with the perfect squares labelled underneath, where a dragged flag is trapped between the two squares that prove the bounds
media.instructions_for_student: A root that is not a whole number still lives somewhere on the line. Find the whole number whose square is just below your number, take the next one up, and the root sits between them. Say both multiplications - one alone proves nothing, because it leaves the root free on the other side. To judge which of the two it is nearer, compare your number with the two SQUARES, not with the two whole numbers. And if your number IS a perfect square, there is nothing to sit between: the root lands on a whole number.

concepts.concept_name: How many unit cubes make a cube

content.text:
1.2 Cubic Numbers
How many cubes of side 1 cm make a cube of side 2 cm? 8.
How many cubes of side 1 cm will make a cube of side 3 cm? 27.
Numbers like 1, 8, 27 are called perfect cubes or cubic numbers. Is 9 a cube? No. In fact no number from 10 to 26 is a cube.
Estimate the number of unit cubes in a cube with an edge of 4 units. There are 4 layers of 16 cubes, so 64.
A cube of edge 5 units has 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 unit cubes. We write n × n × n = n³, read as n cubed.

content.text:
1. Predict first: how many 1 cm cubes build a cube of edge 4 cm? Is it 12, 16 or 64?
2. Build it in layers. The bottom layer is a 4 by 4 square, 16 cubes, and there are 4 layers: 64.
3. So the count is 4 × 4 × 4 = 4³ = 64. Cubing is not multiplying by 3.
4. 2³ = 8 and 3³ = 27, and no number from 9 to 26 can be made into a solid cube.

content.text:
Worked example: How many unit cubes make cubes of edge 2, 3 and 4 units?
1. Edge 2: 2 layers of 2 × 2 = 4 cubes, so 2³ = 8.
2. Edge 3: 3 layers of 3 × 3 = 9 cubes, so 3³ = 27.
3. Edge 4: 4 layers of 4 × 4 = 16 cubes, so 4³ = 64.
Answer: 8, 27 and 64 unit cubes

content.text:
1. Predict first: can a cube end in 7, which no square can?
2. From the table, 1³ = 1, 2³ = 8, 3³ = 27, 7³ = 343: every digit 0 to 9 appears as a last digit.
3. 1 digit: 1 and 8. 2 digits: 27 and 64. 3 digits: 125, 216, 343, 512 and 729.
4. Each zero at the end of the number gives three zeros at the end of its cube, so a cube ends in 0, 3, 6, ... zeros, never exactly two.

content.text:
Worked example: How many cubes have exactly 3 digits, and can a cube end in exactly two zeros?
1. 4³ = 64 has 2 digits and 5³ = 125 has 3 digits.
2. 9³ = 729 has 3 digits and 10³ = 1000 has 4 digits.
3. So the 3 digit cubes are 5³ to 9³: 125, 216, 343, 512 and 729, five cubes.
4. 10³ = 1000 ends in three zeros; each end zero of the number gives three in the cube, so exactly two zeros is impossible.
Answer: Five 3 digit cubes; no cube ends in exactly two zeros

content.text:
Figure it Out (cubic numbers, question 3): State true or false. Explain your reasoning. (i) The cube of any odd number is even. (ii) There is no perfect cube that ends with 8. (iii) The cube of a 2 digit number may be a 3 digit number. (iv) The cube of a 2 digit number may have seven or more digits. (v) Cube numbers have an odd number of factors.
1. (i) False: odd × odd × odd is odd, for example 3³ = 27.
2. (ii) False: 2³ = 8 and 12³ = 1728 end in 8.
3. (iii) False: the smallest 2 digit number is 10, and 10³ = 1000 already has 4 digits.
4. (iv) False: the largest 2 digit number is 99, and 99³ = 970299 has only 6 digits.
5. (v) False: 8 = 2³ has the 4 factors 1, 2, 4 and 8.
Answer: All five statements are false

media.title: Cube Stacker
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Ganita Prakash Ch.1 'A Square and A Cube', the cube half of the chapter. The class has the square array in hand and volume as a count of unit cubes from Class 7; neither is re-taught. Cube roots by prime factorisation come LATER in the same chapter, so the tool never writes the radical sign and asks 'what is its side?' in words instead. It is read at the Build beat of the topic 'Cubes and Their Digits' and rehearses the 1-mark cube-count reading and the 2-mark reverse item directly.

overview.goal: The student builds an n cubed stack in a flat drawing and states the number of unit cubes without counting them one by one.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A flat working surface drawn in a fixed oblique view, the way a stack of dice sits on a table. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class says a cube of side four needs twelve small cubes, and the stack itself is asked to settle it.
overview.concept: A cube of side n is built from n layers, each of which is an n by n square holding n squared unit cubes. The total is therefore n squared taken n times, that is n times n times n, written n cubed. Multiplying by three would give three copies of a length, which is not a solid at all.
overview.purpose: The student builds an n cubed stack in a flat drawing and states the number of unit cubes without counting them one by one.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: The stack fills the main panel with the three readouts in a single row directly beneath it. Add layer and remove layer sit as large buttons below the readouts on a 390 px frame and to the right on a wide frame. Every button keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the total while a prediction is still open, and never draw a layer that is not n by n. The total IS the answer and a non square layer is a lie about the solid.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Each layer is a square of side n and so holds n squared cubes, and there are n such layers stacked to make the height n. Adding n squared to itself n times is n times n squared, which is n cubed. The three readouts are kept separate precisely so that the layer count and the cubes per layer never blur into one number. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the ghost outline of a side 4 cube, nothing built and the total HIDDEN, and asks the class how many small cubes it will need. Beat 2 adds the layers one at a time, each completed layer flashing, with the layer count and the cubes per layer moving separately. Beat 3 hides the total and asks why it is side times side times side rather than side times three, pointing at the layer readout as the evidence. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setSide, addLayer, highlightLayer and say.

Each layer holds n squared, and there are n layers
Cubing is never multiplying by three, at any whole side
conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the ghost outline of a side 4 cube with nothing built and the total hidden, and ask the class to predict the cube count out loud. Commit the class number. Target side 4. Never build before the prediction is committed, and never say 64 at this call. Call 2. Build the four layers one at a time and point at the three readouts as they move. Targets side 4, four layers, 16 cubes per layer. Read the total from the tool's own readout. Call 3. Hide the total again and ask why it is side times side times side rather than side times three, pointing at the layer readout as the evidence. Target the layer that shows 16.

hunts: EQUAL COUNT HUNT: find a square and a cube that hold the same number of units.
TRIPLING HUNT: look for a side where cubing and tripling agree, and say why the search ends empty.
BETWEEN CUBES: pick a total that is not a cube and name the two sides it falls between.
BUILD YOUR OWN: choose any side, predict the total, then build it layer by layer and check.

media.description: A ghost outline of the finished cube stands on a flat working surface in a fixed oblique view, drawn with the unit grid on its three visible faces so the target can be counted before a single cube is placed. Layers of n by n unit cubes then drop into it one at a time, each flashing once in the second accent as it lands, while three separate read-outs move independently: the layer count, the cubes per layer (which does not move at all while layers are added) and the running total. Keeping those three apart is the whole design, because the misconception the tool exists to break is the two factors blurring into one and the raised 3 being read as a multiplier. Concept builds a side-4 cube, rebuilds it layer by layer so the total is seen jumping by a whole 16, and then places only 12 cubes inside the same outline so that 4 x 3 = 12 is visibly three quarters of ONE layer rather than a solid. Learn walks the five reviewed checkpoints, each opening with its own scene and its answer already on screen: one unit cube at side 1, a side-2 stack beside a flat row of 6, a side-2 stack beside the 4 cubes left over from a tray of 12, the full 216 at the draw cap, and a side-4 stack beside a flat 8 by 8 array so both counts land on 64. Practice serves six of the thirty reviewed questions on a difficulty ladder that climbs on a correct answer and drops on a wrong one, with the ghost outline drawn and the total withheld until an attempt is in, and any cube above the side-6 cap drawn as a labelled wireframe so the rule can outlive the picture. Free Play unlocks the side selector, both layer buttons and the outline toggle with nothing scored.

mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the ghost outline of a side 4 cube, nothing built and the total HIDDEN, and asks the class how many small cubes it will need. Beat 2 adds the layers one at a time, each completed layer flashing, with the layer count and the cubes per layer moving separately. Beat 3 hides the total and asks why it is side times side times side rather than side times three, pointing at the layer readout as the evidence. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setSide, addLayer, highlightLayer and say.

concept.notation: Write n cubed, read as 'n cubed' or 'n to the power 3'. The raised 3 counts how many factors of n are multiplied, it is not a multiplier.
concept.statement: A cube of side n is built from n layers, each of which is an n by n square holding n squared unit cubes. The total is therefore n squared taken n times, that is n times n times n, written n cubed. Multiplying by three would give three copies of a length, which is not a solid at all.
prerequisites: square numbers as an n by n array
volume as a count of unit cubes from Class 7
misconceptions: Cubing read as multiplying by three, so 4 cubed is taken as 12.
Confusion of the exponent with a multiplier, so the raised 3 is read as 'times 3'.
concept.why_it_is_true: Each layer is a square of side n and so holds n squared cubes, and there are n such layers stacked to make the height n. Adding n squared to itself n times is n times n squared, which is n cubed. The three readouts are kept separate precisely so that the layer count and the cubes per layer never blur into one number.
worked_numbers: Side 3: three layers of nine, so 27 cubes; multiplying by three would have said 9.
Side 4: four layers of sixteen, so 64 cubes, and the doubling of the side from 2 to 4 multiplies the total by eight, not by two.
Side 6: six layers of thirty six, so 216 cubes, which is the largest stack the tool draws.

answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn stack: the total for the stated side, whether the stated number is a perfect cube, or the side for a stated total.
answer_key.precision: Integer arithmetic only. Totals are exact integer products and cube tests are done by integer search, never by a floating point cube root.
answer_key.ground_truth: total(n) = n * n * n, computed as an integer product. cubesPerLayer(n) = n * n. isPerfectCube(k) = integer search for r in 0..k with r*r*r === k. cubeRoot(k) = that r, or null when none exists.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: One layer of one cube. It is a legal cube and the smallest one, and the three readouts all read 1, which shows the student that cubing leaves 1 unmoved.

The three readouts stay honest: the layer count is what has been built, the cubes per layer is n squared, and the total is what is on screen, not the finished total. The ghost outline shows the target separately.
The stack returns to empty with the ghost outline still present. Empty is a legal state and the tool renders it rather than snapping back to one layer.

edge_cases.case: A number that is not a perfect cube
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The tool refuses to build it as a cube and says why, naming the two whole sides it falls between. It never adds a partial layer to make the total work.
Blocked, with the cap and its reason stated on screen. Above 216 unit faces the oblique drawing stops being readable, so the tool switches to a labelled outline rather than shrinking the cubes.

questions.description: Replaces the built in practice bank. Items are {kind:'count_cubes', n:number} | {kind:'is_cube', k:number} | {kind:'find_side', total:number} | {kind:'choice', prompt, options[], correct, explain}.

startingSide.description: The side the stack opens on, clamped 1 to 6.

showGhostOutline.description: Draw the finished n by n by n cube as a ghost outline before the student builds it, so the target is visible.

constraints: Layers are always n by n. The stack can never become a cuboid, and a move that would make one is refused with the reason on screen.
The drawing is a fixed two dimensional oblique projection. There is no 3D engine and no free rotation.
The oblique offset per depth level is precomputed and the faces are drawn back to front so overlap is correct; the depth ordering is recomputed only when n changes.
At most 216 unit faces are rendered. Above that the stack is drawn as a labelled outline rather than as individual cubes.
The three readouts are separate state fields and are never derived from one another at render time, so a partly built stack cannot report a finished total.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: The oblique stack with its ghost outline, the three readouts, the teacher caption, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: the ghost outline of a side 4 cube is drawn with nothing built and the total HIDDEN. The class commits a cube count out loud and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.
Build: the four layers go in one at a time, each flashing as it completes, with the layer count, the cubes per layer and the total moving in three separate readouts.
Why not three: the total is hidden again and the class is asked why it is side times side times side, with the layer readout tapped as the evidence.

play_modes: EQUAL COUNT HUNT: find a square and a cube that hold the same number of units.
TRIPLING HUNT: look for a side where cubing and tripling agree, and say why the search ends empty.
BETWEEN CUBES: pick a total that is not a cube and name the two sides it falls between.
BUILD YOUR OWN: choose any side, predict the total, then build it layer by layer and check.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example building a side a child names one layer at a time to settle an argument about the exponent.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

lifts the top layer away and lowers the total by n squared

visual_behaviour.never: Do not show the total while a prediction is still open, and never draw a layer that is not n by n. The total IS the answer and a non square layer is a lie about the solid.
visual_behaviour.scene: Unit cubes in a fixed oblique projection, drawn back to front so overlap reads correctly. Built cubes carry the primary accent, the layer that has just completed flashes in the second accent, and the ghost outline of the finished cube stays a thin neutral stroke.
visual_behaviour.layout: The stack fills the main panel with the three readouts in a single row directly beneath it. Add layer and remove layer sit as large buttons below the readouts on a 390 px frame and to the right on a wide frame. Every button keeps a 44 px hit target.
readouts: Cubes per layer, which is n squared and does not move while layers are added
Total cubes on screen, live once the prediction has been committed
animations: Layer drop: a layer descends into place over 220 ms and flashes once on landing, so each layer is registered as one object of n squared cubes.
Layer removal: the top layer lifts and fades over 180 ms, and the total counts down by n squared rather than jumping, so the size of a layer is felt.
Side change: the ghost outline morphs to the new side over 260 ms while the stack empties, which makes plain that layers of the old size do not carry over.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: Unit cube size is derived from the panel width and n so the whole ghost outline fits with its labels legible; above 216 unit faces the individual cubes are dropped and the stack is drawn as a labelled outline.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The three readouts have to be watched moving together before the rule is stated, or side times side times side reads as three numbers multiplied for no reason

mathematical_facts: A cube of side n holds n times n times n unit cubes, written n cubed
Each layer is n by n, so it holds n squared cubes, and there are n layers
Cubing and tripling agree at no whole side at all

question_integration.test: Freeze any injected step and ask: could the teacher read every number in this question off THIS screen? If not, fix the scene, not the words.
question_integration.parse_rule: Read the side out of the question text (the first integer described as a side, an edge or a length) and set n to it. If the question states a total number of cubes or a volume instead, read that and set n to its integer cube root, building the stack only when the root is whole. The stack drawn must contain every number the question mentions.
question_integration.compute_rule: Build the scene from the parsed numbers, then compute the answer with the tool's own ground truth function ON THE DRAWN SCENE. Never carry the bank's answer as truth while drawing a different scene. The two must agree by construction; if they disagree the scene is wrong, not the bank.
question_integration.learn_source: props.learnQuestions (delivery_mode = 'Learn'). Mandatory checkpoints (stickers.mandatory_learn = true) come first, in Easy then Medium then Hard order, and every one of them is served every time the tool loads. The randomly drawn Learn slots follow. The tool NEVER invents a Learn item while the prop is non empty, and never re-orders the mandatory block.
scene_fields: n, the side of the cube
the total, when the question states one
layersBuilt, when the question freezes a partly built stack
question_integration.sceneless_rule: A general claim with no side in it ('why is cubing not the same as multiplying by three?') has nothing to build. Render an authored, self consistent case that exhibits the claim, in this tool a side 4 stack at 64 cubes with the answer 12 drawn beside it as three separate edges, rather than fabricating a scene the question does not describe.
question_integration.practice_source: props.questions (delivery_mode = 'Practice'), drawn at random by the platform inside the difficulty and subtype targets. Mandatory checkpoints are never served here.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 states the idea on a finished stack because the picture has to be believed before it can be argued with: four layers, sixteen in each, sixty-four in all, with the ghost outline still visible around it so the class can see that the stack fills the target exactly.

Beat 2 is the mechanism and it is why the three read-outs are kept apart. The stack empties and rebuilds one layer at a time, and the total moves 16, 32, 48, 64 while 'Cubes per layer' never moves at all. A tripling rule predicts a jump of 4; an adding rule predicts a jump of 4; the screen jumps by 16.

Beat 3 is the chapter's headline error made to fail on screen. Twelve cubes are placed inside the SAME side-4 outline and they do not even fill the bottom layer - the front row of four is missing and three empty layers stand above. Point at the gap, not at the caption.

In Practice, answer each item and press Finish when the bank is done.

media.title: How many unit cubes make cubes of edge 2, 3 and 4?
media.context: A Square and A Cube. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.

media.title: How many cubes have three digits, and can a cube end in two zeros?
media.context: A Square and A Cube. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: The cubes are followed from four cubed to ten cubed to count those with exactly three digits. Then the zeros at the end of ten cubed show how zeros come in a cube. Keeko doubts the zeros, because one hundred seems to be a cube.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: find where the digit count changes, and see that each zero at the end of a number gives three zeros in its cube. Watch for students who think any number ending in zeros is a cube.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students count the unit cubes that make cubes of edge 2, 3 and 4 as layers of squares, write the count with the n cubed notation, and decide whether numbers between cubes can be cubes.
Students use the table of cubes up to 20 to find that cubes can end in any digit, count the cubes with one, two and three digits, and explain why a cube cannot end in exactly two zeros.
Students cube fractions, decimals and negative numbers and explain why the cube of a negative number is negative while its square is positive.
Students stack layers of unit cubes to build cubes of growing edge, read the count as the cube, and test statements about cubes against the stacks.

concepts.concept_name: Taxicab numbers

content.text:
Hardy came to see Ramanujan in a taxi numbered 1729 and remarked that the number seemed rather dull. Ramanujan replied that it is a very interesting number: it is the smallest number expressible as a sum of two cubes in two different ways.
1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³.
Numbers like this are called taxicab numbers. Try this: 4104 = 2³ + 16³ = 9³ + 15³ and 13832 = 2³ + 24³ = 18³ + 20³.
Littlewood said that every positive integer was one of Ramanujan's personal friends.

content.text:
1. Predict first: can 1729 be split into two cubes? Try 12³ first.
2. 12³ = 1728, and 1729 − 1728 = 1 = 1³. So 1729 = 1³ + 12³.
3. Now 10³ = 1000 and 1729 − 1000 = 729 = 9³. A second way: 1729 = 9³ + 10³.
4. 1729 is the smallest number with two such ways; 4104 and 13832 are the next taxicab numbers.

content.text:
Worked example: Show that 4104 is a sum of two cubes in two different ways.
1. 16³ = 4096 and 4104 − 4096 = 8 = 2³, so 4104 = 2³ + 16³.
2. 15³ = 3375 and 4104 − 3375 = 729 = 9³, so 4104 = 9³ + 15³.
3. So 4104 = 2³ + 16³ = 9³ + 15³.
Answer: 4104 = 2³ + 16³ = 9³ + 15³

concepts.concept_name: Cubes from consecutive odd numbers

content.text:
Perfect Cubes and Consecutive Odd Numbers
1 = 1 = 1³, 3 + 5 = 8 = 2³, 7 + 9 + 11 = 27 = 3³, 13 + 15 + 17 + 19 = 64 = 4³, 21 + 23 + 25 + 27 + 29 = 125 = 5³, 31 + 33 + 35 + 37 + 39 + 41 = 216 = 6³.
Using this pattern, find the value of 91 + 93 + 95 + ... + 109 without calculating.

content.text:
1. Predict first: what is 7 + 9 + 11? Is it a square or a cube?
2. Group the odd numbers: 1, then 3 + 5, then 7 + 9 + 11. The sums are 1, 8, 27: the cubes.
3. The nth block has n consecutive odd numbers and adds to n³.
4. 91 to 109 is a block of 10 odd numbers, so it is the 10th block and adds to 10³ = 1000.

content.text:
Worked example: Find 91 + 93 + 95 + 97 + 99 + 101 + 103 + 105 + 107 + 109 using the cube pattern.
1. The blocks of consecutive odd numbers add to 1³, 2³, 3³, and so on.
2. The 9th block ends at 89, so the 10th block runs from 91 to 109: ten odd numbers.
3. The 10th block adds to 10³ = 1000.
4. Check: the numbers pair from the outside to 200 each, 5 pairs, 5 × 200 = 1000.
Answer: 1000
