content.text:
Successive differences: for the squares 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ... the first differences are 3, 5, 7, 9, ... and the second differences are all 2.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the successive differences of the cubes 1, 8, 27, 64, 125 and 216 until they are constant.
1. Level 1: 8 − 1 = 7, 27 − 8 = 19, 64 − 27 = 37, 125 − 64 = 61, 216 − 125 = 91.
2. Level 2: 19 − 7 = 12, 37 − 19 = 18, 61 − 37 = 24, 91 − 61 = 30.
3. Level 3: 18 − 12 = 6, 24 − 18 = 6, 30 − 24 = 6.
4. The differences are constant, 6, at level 3.
Answer: Constant difference 6 at level 3

content.text:
Consecutive squares differ by odd numbers that grow by 2.
Consecutive cubes differ by numbers that grow much faster: 7, 19, 37, 61, 91, ...
The nth cube is the sum of the nth block of n consecutive odd numbers.

content.text:
Figure it Out (cubic numbers, question 5): Which of the following is the greatest? Explain your reasoning. (i) 67³ − 66³ (ii) 43³ − 42³ (iii) 67² − 66² (iv) 43² − 42²
1. Differences of consecutive cubes grow quickly, and they are far bigger than differences of consecutive squares.
2. 67² − 66² = 67 + 66 = 133 and 43² − 42² = 43 + 42 = 85.
3. 43³ − 42³ = 79507 − 74088 = 5419.
4. 67³ − 66³ = 300763 − 287496 = 13267, the greatest.
Answer: (i) 67³ − 66³ is the greatest

concepts.concept_name: Three equal groups of prime factors

content.text:
Cube Roots
The cube root of 8 is 2, the cube root of 27 is 3, and the cube root of 1000 is 10. The cube root of n³ is n. The symbol for the cube root is a root sign with a small 3.
Check if 3375 is a perfect cube. 3375 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 5 × 5 = (3 × 5) × (3 × 5) × (3 × 5), so 3375 = 15³ and its cube root is 15.
Is 500 a perfect cube? 500 = 2 × 2 × 5 × 5 × 5. The 2s cannot be put into three equal groups, so 500 is not a perfect cube.

content.text:
1. Predict first: is 3375 a perfect cube? Its last digit is 5, so its root would end in 5.
2. Factorise: 3375 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 5 × 5. Each prime appears three times.
3. Split into three equal groups, 3 × 5 in each: 3375 = 15 × 15 × 15, so the cube root is 15.
4. 500 = 2 × 2 × 5 × 5 × 5: only two 2s, so 500 is not a perfect cube.

content.text:
Worked example: Decide whether 3375 and 500 are perfect cubes, and give the cube root of the one that is.
1. 3375 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 5 × 5.
2. Three equal groups of 3 × 5 = 15, so 3375 = 15 × 15 × 15 = 15³.
3. 500 = 2 × 2 × 5 × 5 × 5; two 2s cannot make three equal groups.
4. So 3375 is a perfect cube with cube root 15, and 500 is not a perfect cube.
Answer: 3375 = 15³, cube root 15; 500 is not a perfect cube

content.text:
Worked example: Find the cube roots of 64, 512 and 729.
1. 64 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = (2 × 2) × (2 × 2) × (2 × 2), so its cube root is 4.
2. 512 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 × 8 × 8, so its cube root is 8.
3. 729 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 9 × 9 × 9, so its cube root is 9.
Answer: The cube roots are 4, 8 and 9

content.text:
A perfect cube has every prime factor appearing a multiple of three times.
One of the three equal groups, multiplied out, is the cube root.
Multiplying by the missing primes completes the groups.

content.text:
Figure it Out (cubic numbers, question 1): Find the cube roots of 27000 and 10648.
1. 27000 = 27 × 1000 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 × 5 × 5.
2. Three equal groups of 3 × 2 × 5 = 30, so the cube root of 27000 is 30.
3. 10648 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 11 × 11 × 11.
4. Three equal groups of 2 × 11 = 22, so the cube root of 10648 is 22.
Answer: 30 and 22

media.title: Cube Root Tripler
media.context: CBSE Class 8, A Square and A Cube, cube roots by prime factorisation. It follows the pairing mount directly, so the surface is deliberately identical and what the student has to supply is the change from two to three, not a new procedure. NCERT states the rule as a COUNT - each factor appearing three times - so the flat repeated product stays on screen beside the exponent form, and the radical is written as the cube root sign the class has met, never as a fractional power.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the grouping that explains it.
whatYouLearned: A number is a perfect cube exactly when every exponent is a multiple of three
The cube root is one tile from each ring, multiplied together
A leftover prime can cost two more copies, so the cube repair differs from the square repair

overview.goal: The student groups prime factors in threes to find a cube root, and explains why the groups are threes and not twos.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: The same loose rail of prime factor tiles as the pairing mount, with a small oblique cube rebuilding beside it. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: The pairing method has just worked for squares, and the class is asked what has to change for cubes.
overview.concept: A number is a perfect cube exactly when every prime in its factorisation appears a number of times that is a multiple of three, because the tiles can then be split into three identical groups and each group multiplies to the cube root. The square case needed twos because a square is two equal factors; the cube case needs threes because a cube is three.
overview.purpose: The student groups prime factors in threes to find a cube root, and explains why the groups are threes and not twos.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Tile rail fills the main panel with the cube picture to its right on a wide frame and directly beneath it on a 390 px frame. The verdict strip and the multiply box sit under the rail. Draggable tiles are never placed closer than 60 px apart. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the verdict, the cube root or the rebuilt cube while a prediction is still open, and never draw a ring of two tiles. A ring of two is the misconception, not a stage on the way.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. If every exponent is a multiple of three, the tiles split into three identical groups whose common product is some s, so the original number is s times s times s. If some exponent is not a multiple of three, no such split exists, because one group would have to hold more copies of that prime than another. The multiplier that repairs it supplies exactly enough copies to bring each exponent up to the next multiple of three, and nothing more. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

media.description: Prime factor tiles lie on a rail, exactly the surface the pairing tool used for square roots, and the one thing that changes is the size of a group: a ring holds THREE copies of the same prime, and a trio that is not three of a kind shakes, springs apart and states why. A small oblique unit cube stands beside the rail and rebuilds at the side the closed rings give, so the grouping and the solid finish together. The number and its factorisation are always on screen in both forms the textbook uses - the flat repeated product 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 3 and the exponent form 2 cubed times 3 cubed - and the cube root is announced only as the product of one tile from each ring, never computed by a floating point cube root. Concept runs three beats: 216 ringed in threes with its root read off the rings; the same six tiles PAIRED in twos beside them, giving 6 x 6 = 36 with two tiles left over, so the habit from the square case visibly fails; then 128, which leaves one 2 over, where multiplying by 2 is TRIED and still leaves tiles loose while only 4 empties the rail. Learn walks the five reviewed checkpoints answered. Practice serves six of a thirty item pool on a difficulty ladder, hiding the quantity it asks for until an attempt is in. Free Play lets the child type any number up to a million, ring and unring at will, multiply by anything, and say in their own words what changed from the square case.

concept.notation: Write the factorisation with exponents, for example 216 as 2 cubed times 3 cubed. The cube root is written as the product of one prime from each group of three.
concept.statement: A number is a perfect cube exactly when every prime in its factorisation appears a number of times that is a multiple of three, because the tiles can then be split into three identical groups and each group multiplies to the cube root. The square case needed twos because a square is two equal factors; the cube case needs threes because a cube is three.
prerequisites: prime factorisation and pairing for square roots
cube numbers as n times n times n
misconceptions: Cube root treated as one third of the number, so the cube root of 27 is taken as 9.
The pairing method copied across without understanding the exponent link, so tiles are grouped in twos out of habit.
concept.why_it_is_true: If every exponent is a multiple of three, the tiles split into three identical groups whose common product is some s, so the original number is s times s times s. If some exponent is not a multiple of three, no such split exists, because one group would have to hold more copies of that prime than another. The multiplier that repairs it supplies exactly enough copies to bring each exponent up to the next multiple of three, and nothing more.
worked_numbers: 216 is 2 cubed times 3 cubed, so it groups cleanly and its cube root is 2 times 3, that is 6.
1728 is 2 to the sixth times 3 cubed, giving two groups of 2 and one of 3, so its cube root is 4 times 3, that is 12.
108 is 2 squared times 3 cubed: the two 2s are short of a group, so multiplying by 2 gives 216 and a cube root of 6.

answer_key.worked: A number is a perfect cube exactly when every prime appears a number of times that is a multiple of three, and the cube root is the product of one prime from each group.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn tile set: whether every exponent is a multiple of three, the cube root read off as one tile from each group, or the smallest multiplier that completes every group.
answer_key.precision: Integer arithmetic only, with factorisation by trial division up to the integer square root. No floating point cube root decides any graded value.
answer_key.ground_truth: factorise(k) = trial division by d from 2 while d*d <= k, returning a Map from prime to exponent. isCube(k) = every exponent is a multiple of 3. cubeRoot(k) = product of p to the power e/3 over the map, computed only when isCube(k). smallestMultiplier(k) = product over primes of p to the power ((3 - e mod 3) mod 3).

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The tile set is empty and every exponent is vacuously a multiple of three, so 1 is a perfect cube with cube root 1. The tool states this rather than treating an empty set as an error.
Blocked before factorising, with the reason on screen. Zero has no prime factorisation to group, so the tool refuses rather than drawing an empty rail and calling it a cube.

edge_cases.case: A group of the wrong size
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: A ring holding two or four tiles shakes and separates, with the reason stated. A group must hold exactly three identical primes, and the refusal is where the rule is taught.
One tile, never a full group, so it is never a cube and the smallest multiplier is the prime squared. This is the case that most clearly separates the cube rule from the square rule.

edge_cases.case: An exponent that is a multiple of six
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The number is both a square and a cube. The tool says so, which is the link forward to the sorting tool rather than a coincidence to be passed over.

constraints: The multiset of prime tiles always multiplies back to the original number. A grouping move can never change the product.

practice.shows: The item's own tile set, the question, the answer affordance, a running score, and the Finish button.
steps: One item at a time from props.questions; the tool never re-orders or filters the bank.
practice.review: The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the grouping that explains it.
practice.done_when: The bank is exhausted (emit bank_done, not terminal) or the student presses Finish (emit finished, once).
practice.opens_with: Item 1 of the bank, tiles laid out ungrouped, verdict hidden, score at 0.

interactions.trigger: Drag three tiles into a ring
interactions.feedback: A refused ring states that a group must hold exactly three copies of the same prime, so the difference from the square case is taught by the refusal.
interactions.response: Three identical primes lock into one ring; a ring of any other size shakes and separates.

interactions.trigger: Tap a group to break it
interactions.feedback: The running count of grouped and loose tiles updates, so undoing does not lose the verdict.
interactions.response: The ring opens and the three tiles return to the loose rail.

interactions.feedback: The cube root is announced as the product of one tile from each group, so the number and the picture arrive as the same fact.
interactions.response: The small oblique cube rebuilds beside the tiles at the side given by the cube root.

interactions.trigger: State what changes between the square case and the cube case
interactions.feedback: The tool does not mark the sentence. It is the transfer of the structural idea that the agent reviews, not a new procedure to be scored.
interactions.response: The typed sentence is stored verbatim and passed to the agent, unrepaired and ungraded by the tool.

interactions.feedback: Correct locks the grouping and the rebuilt cube open as the explanation; wrong replays the grouping with the student's answer shown alongside the true one.
interactions.response: The verdict, the cube root or the multiplier is checked against the tool's own ground truth on the drawn tile set.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example grouping a number a child names and showing how many tiles are short of a full three.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

steps: Cubing equals tripling would need n times n times n to equal 3 times n.

steps: A ring needs three copies of the prime, and only one copy is left over.
So two more 2s are needed, which is 2 times 2, that is 4.
128 times 4 is 512.
8 times 8 times 8 is 512, so the product is a perfect cube.
For a square one leftover costs one more copy; for a cube it can cost two.

visual_behaviour.never: Do not show the verdict, the cube root or the rebuilt cube while a prediction is still open, and never draw a ring of two tiles. A ring of two is the misconception, not a stage on the way.
visual_behaviour.scene: Prime factor tiles on a loose rail, identical in form to the pairing tool so the transfer is visible. A completed group is drawn as one ring of three tiles in the primary accent; loose tiles stay outlined. A small oblique unit cube sits beside the rail and rebuilds as the grouping completes.
visual_behaviour.layout: Tile rail fills the main panel with the cube picture to its right on a wide frame and directly beneath it on a 390 px frame. The verdict strip and the multiply box sit under the rail. Draggable tiles are never placed closer than 60 px apart.
readouts: The number and its factorisation as a product of primes, always on screen
How many tiles are grouped and how many are loose, live
The cube root, or the smallest multiplier, once every group is complete
animations: Group close: three identical tiles rotate into a ring over 220 ms, which reads as one object of three rather than as a chain of two joins.
Refused ring: a group of the wrong size shakes over 200 ms and springs apart with the reason stated, so an illegal move is answered rather than silently undone.
Cube rebuild: as each group closes, one more layer of the small oblique cube appears, so the grouping and the solid finish at the same instant.
visual_behaviour.scale_rule: Tile size is derived from the panel width and the tile count so every prime stays at least 16 px and every tile keeps a 44 px hit target; above 24 tiles the rail wraps rather than shrinking the tiles, and the cube picture caps at 216 unit faces.

teaching_sequence.rationale: The student already owns pairing from the previous mount, so the cube case is best met as a stated change to a method they have, then tested on the tiles

tool_config.image_prompts_note: Empty by design. This mount is a mechanism, not a depiction, and the standard mandates hand-built inline SVG with no external asset dependency, so no depictive picture is declared.
mathematical_facts: A number is a perfect cube exactly when every prime appears a multiple of three times
The cube root is the product of one tile from each complete group of three
A single leftover prime needs two more copies before its group closes, so the multiplier is that prime squared

question_integration.test: Freeze any injected step and ask: could the teacher read every number in this question off THIS screen? If not, fix the scene, not the words.
question_integration.parse_rule: Read the number out of the question text (the first integer described as a number, a value or the thing being tested) and set number to it, refusing 0 and anything above 10 to the power 6. If the question names a multiplier, apply it only after the base factorisation is on screen. The tile set drawn must account for every prime the question mentions.
question_integration.compute_rule: Build the scene from the parsed numbers, then compute the answer with the tool's own ground truth function ON THE DRAWN SCENE. Never carry the bank's answer as truth while drawing a different scene. The two must agree by construction; if they disagree the scene is wrong, not the bank.

Mandatory checkpoints (stickers.mandatory_learn = true) come first, in Easy then Medium then Hard order, and every one of them is served every time the tool loads. The randomly drawn Learn slots follow. The tool NEVER invents a Learn item while the prop is non empty, and never re-orders the mandatory block.
scene_fields: the multiplier, when the question states one
showCubePicture, on when the question refers to the solid
question_integration.sceneless_rule: A general claim with no number in it ('why threes and not twos?') has nothing to group. Render an authored, self consistent case that exhibits the claim, in this tool 216 grouped in threes beside the same tiles paired in twos and visibly failing, rather than fabricating a scene the question does not describe.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 states the idea on the tiles: 216 rings into three 2s and three 3s, and the root is one tile from each ring multiplied together. Point at each ring and let the class read its own product aloud before naming 6, so the root arrives as a product of rings and not as a remembered fact.

Beat 2 is the whole argument, and it is a REFUTATION. The same six tiles are drawn paired in twos above and ringed in threes below. Pairing gives 6 x 6 = 36, which is not 216, and leaves two tiles stranded; ringing gives 6 x 6 x 6 = 216 with nothing over. The habit carried across from square roots fails on the screen rather than being denied in a caption.

Beat 3 prices a leftover, and the student's own guess is tried first. 128 is 2 to the seventh: two rings and one 2 over. The strip shows 128 x 2 = 256 STILL leaving two tiles loose, and only 128 x 4 = 512 emptying the rail. That is the whole difference from the square repair, and it is shown as a failed attempt, never asserted.
media.generation_prompt: Cube Root Tripler: the same prime tile surface as the pairing tool but grouped in threes, with a small oblique cube rebuilding beside the tiles whenever the grouping completes
media.instructions_for_student: A ring holds three tiles of the same prime, because a cube is three equal factors. Tap three matching tiles to close a ring; tap a closed ring to open it again. When every tile is in a ring, the cube root is one tile from each ring, multiplied together. If tiles are left over the number is not a cube yet - work out how many more copies each short prime needs to reach a multiple of three, and that product is the smallest multiplier.

concepts.concept_name: Cubic Numbers, Q2

content.text:
Figure it Out (cubic numbers, question 2): What number will you multiply by 1323 to make it a cube number?
1. 1323 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 7 × 7.
2. The 3s make a full group of three; the 7s need one more 7.
3. 1323 × 7 = 9261 = 3 × 3 × 3 × 7 × 7 × 7 = 21³.
Answer: Multiply by 7, giving 9261 = 21³

concepts.concept_name: Cubic Numbers, Q4

content.text:
Figure it Out (cubic numbers, question 4): Guess the cube roots of the following numbers: (i) 1331 (ii) 4913 (iii) 12167 (iv) 32768
1. 1331 ends in 1 and lies between 10³ = 1000 and 20³ = 8000; 11³ = 1331.
2. 4913 ends in 3, and only 7³ ends in 3 among 1 to 9, so try 17: 17³ = 4913.
3. 12167 lies between 20³ = 8000 and 30³ = 27000 and ends in 7, so try 23: 23³ = 12167.
4. 32768 lies between 30³ = 27000 and 40³ = 64000 and ends in 8, so try 32: 32³ = 32768.
Answer: (i) 11 (ii) 17 (iii) 23 (iv) 32

concepts.concept_name: What we found about squares and cubes

content.text:
A number obtained by multiplying a number by itself is called a square number.
Squares of natural numbers are called perfect squares. All perfect squares end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9.
Square numbers can be written as the sum of consecutive odd numbers starting with 1.
Finding the square root is the inverse operation of squaring.
A number obtained by multiplying a number by itself three times is called a cube number.
Cube numbers can be written as the sum of consecutive odd numbers.
Finding the cube root is the inverse operation of cubing; prime factorisation helps find square roots and cube roots.

concepts.concept_name: A pinch of history: varga, ghana and mula

content.text:
1.3 A Pinch of History
Clay tablets from Babylon, from around 1700 BCE, list squares and cubes of numbers.
In India the square was called varga and the cube ghana, and the fourth power varga-varga. Aryabhata, in 499 CE, explained varga as the area of a square figure and ghana as the volume of a cube with equal sides.
The word mula, meaning the root of a plant, was used for the root of a number: varga-mula for the square root and ghana-mula for the cube root. Brahmagupta, in 628 CE, also used pada for the square root.
The word passed into Arabic as jidhr and into Latin as radix, the root of a plant, which is where our word root comes from.

concepts.concept_name: Square Pairs

content.text:
Puzzle Time: Square Pairs!
In the row 3, 6, 10, 15, 1, each pair of neighbours adds up to a perfect square: 3 + 6 = 9, 6 + 10 = 16, 10 + 15 = 25, 15 + 1 = 16.
Arrange the numbers 1 to 17, without repeating, in a row so that each pair of neighbours adds up to a perfect square.
Can you arrange the numbers 1 to 32 in a circle so that each pair of neighbours adds up to a perfect square?

content.text:
1. Predict first: which numbers from 1 to 17 can sit next to 16?
2. Neighbour sums can only be 4, 9, 16 or 25. 16 pairs only with 9 to make 25, and 17 only with 8.
3. A number with only one possible neighbour must sit at an end, so 16 and 17 are the two ends.
4. Build inwards from both ends, checking each sum.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students restate how squares and cubes are formed, the patterns and digit facts they follow, and the methods for finding square roots and cube roots.

objectives.objective_text: Students list the people who toggle a given locker, recognise them as the factors of the locker number, and pair each factor with its partner factor.
Students find the numbers whose factors do not all pair with a different partner, explain that a factor multiplied by itself has no separate partner, and name such numbers square numbers.
Students list the lockers that stay open after all 100 people pass as the square numbers up to 100.
Students decide for any locker number how many times it is toggled by counting its factors, and find the lockers touched exactly twice as the prime numbers.
Students find the area of squares of given sides, write the result with the n squared notation, and extend squaring to fractions and decimals.
Students show from the table that squares end only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9, that such an ending does not guarantee a square, and predict the last digit of a square.
Students list squares ending in 1 from numbers ending in 1 or 9 and write numbers ruled out as squares by their units digit alone.

Students predict how many zeros end the square of a number ending in zeros, explain why a square always ends in an even number of zeros, and show that a number and its square are both odd or both even.
Students build squares of tiles of growing side, read the area as the square, and use the last digit, the end zeros and the parity to decide quickly whether a number can be a square.
Students find the differences between consecutive squares, recognise them as the odd numbers, and explain with the inverted L picture why the first n odd numbers add to n squared.
Students subtract 1, 3, 5 and so on from a number in turn and decide it is a perfect square exactly when the subtractions reach 0, counting the steps to find the root.
Students find the nth odd number as 2n − 1 and use it to get the next square from a given square.
Students use the odd number pattern to get squares from neighbouring squares and to check number patterns built from squares.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
Students count the numbers strictly between consecutive squares, find that there are 2n between n squared and the next square, and explain the count with the odd number gap.
Students count the perfect squares in each block of 100 numbers up to 1000, explain why the count drops, and find the largest square below 1000.
Students list the triangular numbers, add consecutive pairs, and explain with a dot picture why each sum is a perfect square.
Students count the numbers between consecutive squares for large squares using 2n instead of listing.
Students find the side of a square of given area, describe finding a square root as the reverse of squaring, and explain why 64 has the two square roots 8 and −8.
Students rule out numbers as squares by their last digit and find the square root of a perfect square by listing the squares of numbers close to its root.
Students find the square root of a perfect square by counting the consecutive odd numbers subtracted to reach 0, and judge when this method is too slow.
Students resize a square to match a given area, read off the side as the square root, and see that an area that is not a perfect square has a side between two whole numbers.
Students factorise a number into primes, split the primes into two identical groups when possible, and conclude whether the number is a perfect square and what its root is.
Students factorise 1156 and 2800 into primes and use the pairing test to decide which is a perfect square.
Students drag prime factors into pairs, decide whether a number is a perfect square, and find the smallest multiplier or divisor that leaves every prime paired.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
Students locate the root of a large perfect square between two multiples of 10, narrow it to two candidates with the last digit, and choose by comparing with the square of the middle number.
Students trap the square root of a number that is not a perfect square between two consecutive whole numbers and say which one it is closer to.
Students decide whether a square of a given whole number side can be cut from a square cloth of given area, and find the largest whole number side possible.
Students slide two whole number bounds until their squares trap a given number, decide whether it is a perfect square, and say which bound the root is closer to.
Students count the unit cubes that make cubes of edge 2, 3 and 4 as layers of squares, write the count with the n cubed notation, and decide whether numbers between cubes can be cubes.
Students use the table of cubes up to 20 to find that cubes can end in any digit, count the cubes with one, two and three digits, and explain why a cube cannot end in exactly two zeros.
Students cube fractions, decimals and negative numbers and explain why the cube of a negative number is negative while its square is positive.
Students stack layers of unit cubes to build cubes of growing edge, read the count as the cube, and test statements about cubes against the stacks.
Students verify that 1729, 4104 and 13832 can each be written as a sum of two cubes in two different ways.
Students group the odd numbers into blocks of 1, 2, 3, ... numbers, find that each block adds to a cube, and use the pattern to add a block of ten odd numbers without adding term by term.
Students take differences of consecutive squares and of consecutive cubes level by level until they become constant, and compare the level at which each becomes constant.
Students use the difference patterns of squares and cubes to compare differences of consecutive powers without computing every power.
Students find the cube root of a number by splitting its prime factors into three identical groups, and decide that a number is not a perfect cube when they cannot.
Students find the cube roots of 64, 512 and 729 by grouping prime factors in threes, using the table of cube factorisations.
Students sort prime factors into three identical groups to find cube roots, and find the smallest multiplier that completes the groups to make a perfect cube.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
Attempt each practice question independently, working through every step before viewing the video solution and checking the answer.
Students restate how squares and cubes are formed, the patterns and digit facts they follow, and the methods for finding square roots and cube roots.
